speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CALL FOR CREATION OF QUEEN CHARLOTTE ISLANDS PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of the House the situation in South Moresby in the Queen Charlotte Islands. I had the opportunity last week, along with my wife and other friends, including Bill Reid, the famous Haida artist, to sail for six days around the South Moresby parts of the Queen Charlottes visiting the traditional Haida sites, seeing the most magnificient primeval forest on the face of the globe, which is really an environmental treasure. There is limitless aquaculture, among the richest in the world. It is nesting grounds for hundreds of varieties of birds.
This, of course, is the traditional home of the Haida nation.
For over 4,000 to 6,000 years they have lived there and built up a unique culture and tradition, and depended upon the resources of the islands and the sea for their livelihood. That is all threatened, of course, by prospective off shore drilling. It is also threatened by indiscriminate logging, particularly on Lyell Island and, potentially, some of the rest of South Moresby. If this continue indiscriminately, the country will lose a priceless heritage.
I wish to suggest to the new Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and congratulate him upon his appointment, that he, buttressed by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), negotiate with the Province of British Columbia for a national park, recognizing the traditional rights of the Haida people in such negotiations and making an accommodation with the logging industry so that selective logging can still take place in other parts of the islands.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: S O. 22 WOMEN SEXUAL VIOLENCE STATISTICS
S O. 22 WOMEN SEXUAL VIOLENCE STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the annual Take Back the Night Marches being held across the country this weekend and next weekend serve to highlight the pervasive problem of violence in our society. Studies indicate that 83 per cent of women have experienced sexual violence and that violence of this kind is on the increase. Indeed, the statistics are chillingly familiar. One woman in ten is beaten by her husband or mate, and a rape is committed every half hour in this country. According to Pierre-Marc Johnson, the Quebec Justice Minister, some 256,000 in that province alone are chronically beaten.
Unfortunately the Conservative Government to date has done little to respond to the plight of Canadian women. As part of its election platform, the Tories promised to increase funding to sexual assault centres which provide essential counselling and support services for the victims of sexual violence. To date we have seen no action taken on this promise. In fact the Tories have indicated their intention to cut transfer payments to the provinces. Rather than providing greater support to sexual assault centres, this may have the effect of a reduction in funding for transition houses and other shelters for battered women. Nor has the Government seen fit to provide adequate funds for research on batterers. Given the documented increase of violence against women at all levels of our society, this oversight is inexcusable.
We call upon the Government to take urgent action on this serious problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: NEED TO ENSURE SURVIVAL OF DOMINION TEXTILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to the situation now prevailing in the Canadian textile and clothing industry, and voice the concerns of employees in the industry, business people, mayors and chambers of commerce in the Valleyfield area and the population in general.
Not long ago, Canada's biggest textile manufacturer, Dominion Textiles in Montreal, announced it was closing its plants in Saint-Jean and Valleyfield, thus adding to a long list of shutdowns and jobs lost in the textile sector.
Mr. Speaker, Dominion Textiles maintains it had no choice but to proceed with these shutdowns, considering the dramatic increase in clothing imports in Canada since 1979.
Despite an ambitious program, the industry has been unable to compete with foreign imports, especially from countries with low labour costs.
We have no reason to believe that the industry alone will be able to improve its competitive position in the foreseeable future.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I want to ask the Minister responsible for these issues to immediately take steps to ensure the survival of an industry that employs more than 170,000 people in Canada, 90,000 of whom work in Quebec.
Finally, I want to ask the Minister of Regional industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to provide for a long-term textile and clothing policy. Such a policy would ensure that Canadian manufacturers have a share of the domestic market, thus guaranteeing the industry's viability in this country.
Mr. Speaker, the future does not look promising.

speechtext:

speechtext:

September 13, 1985

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE-STATEMENT MADE BY NDP MEMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in this House, while discussing the controversial Gibbons Bill now before the U.S. Congress, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) stated that our Government was not doing enough to prevent this legislation. And I quote from Hansard at page 6539:
Surely ... the Prime Minister ... has awakened to the economic guillotine raised by the Gibbons Bill.
I travelled with the Hon. Member for Skeena to Washington this summer to discuss the issue of countervailing duties against our softwood lumber products with a group of American Congressmen. Our Government invited the Hon. Member for Skeena to take part in even further discussions with Congressman Gibbons in Vancouver last month.
The Hon. Member knows that we are very much aware of the inherent dangers in protectionist legislation south of the forty-ninth parallel, but when he talks of "waking up" to the issues, perhaps he should counsel his own Party and, while he is at it, the Liberal Party as well.
Those Hon. Members have to learn that they cannot continue to talk out of both sides of their mouths when it comes to the Americans. There is a iplace for valid criticism but you cannot attack the United States on the one hand, abusing, demeaning, and insulting it, while on the other hand you are pleading with it to buy our B.C. lumber. These people are our friends and our greatest market-place. They have no friends in the New Democratic Party or the Liberal Party. What the opposition Parties have to wake up to, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that, when you talk out of both sides of your mouth, people stop listening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the summer the people of northeastern Nova Scotia, who are already hard hit by the Government's Budget, received yet another economic blow. Canadian National Railways, the biggest customer of the idle Sydney Steel Corporation, announced in July that it had decided to purchase almost 30,000 tonnes of rails from foreign suppliers.
CN officials also confirmed at that time that its purchase of rail from Sydney Steel for the coming year would be down significantly, indeed, that it would actually be less than one-third of the tonnage which CN purchased from Sysco last year. While Rome burns, the Government and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) continue to fiddle. At the time of the announcement the Minister even admitted that he was completely unaware of CN's decision to buy rail from foreign sources. subsubtopic: REPRESENTATION IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday we learned that Canadians from visible minority communities represent only 1.7 per cent of all employees within the federal Public Service. The under-representation of visible minorities within the federal Public Service was not a well concealed secret. Monday's findings, however, clearly demonstrate the alarming degree of this imbalance, especially when one considers that the presence of visible minorities within the Canadian labour force is estimated at 4 per cent.
In response, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced a number of measures. While they are no doubt a beginning, they largely focus on data collection and monitoring rather than on immediate hiring and training and a workplace free of discrimination.
If the Government is to encourage other levels of government and the private sector to pursue employment equity successfully, then bold and decisive action should be the order of the day. In June of last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) declared: "I believe there is no obligation more compelling and no duty more irresistible than to ensure our minorities live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice." It would be highly appropriate for the Conservative Government to recall those words, for Canadians are anxiously waiting for these statements to be translated quickly into reality. Surely the time for platitudes is over.

Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to the House about apartheid and about what Canada can do to end a repugnant racist system. I am guided by two realities: first, that Canadians are offended by, and abhor, the practice of institutionalized racism by a society which claims to share our values; and, second, that Canada's influence is limited but real, and our challenge is to take practical steps which help to end apartheid.
Expressing our outrage is part of our duty and those Canadians citizens who join in peaceful protest and demonstration help to show the South African Government how deeply the people of this country are offended by their racist practices.
It is also part of our duty to make clear to South Africa that Canada is prepared to invoke total sanctions if there is no change. As a general principle, we believe that diplomatic and economic relations should exist even though Governments might disagree. Indeed, if we had accepted six months ago the advice of some groups that we break all diplomatic and commercial relations with South Africa, we would be in no position today to act individually or in concert with other nations to add to the pressure being felt by the South African Government.
We fully recognize, however, that Canada has a responsibility to provide both moral and practical leadership. The Government of South Africa should have no doubt that we will invoke full sanctions unless there is tangible movement away from apartheid.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I will be reviewing today the actions Canada has taken, announcing new initiatives and asking the House to consider avenues of influence which we, our fellow citizens and our friends in the world can pursue. However, first, I think it helpful to indicate some of the changes we seek to bring on those norms of behaviour we expect of all civilized countries, changes which would prove that South Africa is moving away from apartheid. [Translation]
The changes we are seeking include first of all, establishing common citizenship, which means the same political rights, including voting rights, for all and eliminating the different
classes of citizens.
Statements by Ministers
Second, abolishing the laws by which South Africans are classified according to colour or race. Third, freedom for all South Africans to live, travel and work without being subject to arbitrary constraints.
Fourth, independence for Namibia in accordance with United Nations Resolution 435. This would be a major indication that South Africa is willing to accept its neighbours and live on peaceful terms with them. However, the most important points are those I am about to announce now.
First, liberation of political prisoners-the liberation of the leaders of the African National Congress and the United Democratic Front who were forced to resist the apartheid system.
Second, the establishing of a process of consultation and negotiation with the true leaders of those who are referred to as Indians, blacks and coloureds. In other words, such consultations cannot be restricted to the leaders of the Homelands. [English]
Finally, the initiation of a process of reform based on consent, not imposition or coercion. Such a process would clearly lead to representative institutions which include blacks. These are key steps, for it is not Canada's or any other country's consent or support which is crucial to this process. It is the consent and support of South Africans of every race and colour which counts.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
What we are witnessing in South Africa, rather than change, is a deepening crisis. Demonstrations, strikes and acts of resistance against an injust system continue. They continue to be met with violence, arbitrary arrest and detention-measures of repression and control rather than conciliation.
We condemn the detention of the leaders of the United Democratic Front-Professor Farouk Meer, and others. We are shocked by the detention of Allan Boesak, the President of the World Alliance of Reformed Churches, who a short while ago visited Canada and spoke to us not of revolution or violence, but of justice, equality and reconciliation. We deplore the heartlessness of a Government which keeps behind bars the now seriously ill Nelson Mandela.
We call on the South African Government to release all those whose offence is simply to oppose apartheid.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:

September 13, 1985
Statements by Ministers
Bishop Tutu can no doubt bear his rebuff from President Botha. Both Nelson Mandela and Allan Boesak may bear their imprisonment. But can South Africa bear the result? It is clear that one more community in South Africa, the business community, is beginning to have its doubts. Their confidence shaken, business and investors within and outside South Africa have fostered a wave of disinvestment-without the prompting of Governments, but surely reflecting both the events on the ground in South Africa and the signals many Governments have sent. If some South African entrepreneurs have, for too long, lent support to apartheid, the consequence of their movement now cannot be overstated.
Canada's contribution to bringing about those new realities, recognized by South African businessmen, has been significant. Our policy, through several administrations, has been one of consistent opposition to apartheid.
More recently, at Baie Comeau on July 6, I issued a statement of policy on behalf of the Government of Canada. Basing ourselves not on our own righteousness, but on our common humanity, we introduced 10 steps, including certain economic sanctions, to strengthen our opposition to apartheid, and two measures to foster peaceful change.
We ended the Program for Export Market Development and the global insurance policies written by the Export Development Corporation in so far as they applied to South Africa. That lived up to the pledges of the former Government and stopped all official support for trade and investment in South Africa. These two trade measures sent very distinct signals.
We broadened and tightened application of the United Nations arms embargo so as to include a broader range of high-technology items, including computers. We have been the only Government to announce the abrogation of our Double Taxation Agreements.

We have drawn the attention of Canadians to the resolution of the Security Council prohibiting the sale of the krugerrand. We were not disappointed in our hopes that the people selling these gold coins in Canada would get the message, since sales have practically ceased altogether.
We have drafted policies on sports events, official meetings and co-operation. We have made it known that the custom processing of Namibian uranium would come to an end upon expiry of current contracts, at whatever cost.
We have announced the appointment to our embassy in South Africa of an officer responsible for labour issues, in order to maintain direct contacts with those South African workers who support reform. The officer will be selected in consultation with the Canadian Labour Congress.
We have more than tripled funds earmarked for the education and training of blacks, which means we will be able to provide 40 bursaries during the present financial year. We are delighted with the Canadian labour movement's decision to
support the training of blacks in South Africa, and we shall welcome any initiative or contribution from other sources. [English]
But that has not been all. Other levels of Government have also sent strong signals. A number of provinces have seen this as a special case and have shown by their actions that Canadians in all parts of our country abhor apartheid. In addition, private Canadian companies have voluntarily announced that they will no longer purchase South African products. Canadian labour has consistently spoken out against apartheid, and now some Canadian unions have refused to unload a ship carrying South African steel. Universities are debating disinvestment of their South African holdings. This issue has, in a dramatic manner, affected Canadians as a people, and South Africans who condone apartheid should know that they offend not just the Government of Canada, but our people and our values.	*
In focusing that anger, in applying steady pressure for change, we must have the best information and judgments we can get on how to use our influence most effectively. We will work closely with our friends. The distinguished African leader, the Chairman of the Front Line States, President Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, has been invited by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to pay an official visit to Canada which will take place from September 24 to September 26. The Secretary General of the Commonwealth will visit Canada in early October. We will seek their advice and that of other leaders opposed to apartheid, particularly in the Commonwealth and among the front line states. We expect the meeting of the heads of government of the Commonwealth in mid-October to provide an opportunity for common action against apartheid.
We are taking a number of further measures as the Government of Canada as part of our continuing pressure against apartheid. First, as I believe the House knows, 1 am meeting with a number of representatives of Canadian business and finance in order to examine areas of co-operative action against apartheid because I believe that there is a very real possibility that where Governments may not have influence on some levels of the business community and the bureaucracy in South Africa, Canadians active in business could well have the influence which could add to what Governments, Parliament and public officials are trying to do.
The first meeting took place on September 9. The others will follow shortly, on September 17 and September 20.
Second, the Canadian Government is introducing a voluntary ban on loans to the Government of South Africa and all of its agencies. We are asking all Canadian banks to apply such a ban and we have reason to believe that they will do so. Some have already acted on their own and we welcome that. The ban will not affect any outstanding credits nor prevent loans that would clearly be to the benefit of blacks.
Third, I am announcing the appointment of Mr. Albert Hart as administrator of the Canadian code of conduct for the employment practices of Canadian companies operating in South Africa. Mr. Hart has had a distinguished career as a
September 13, 1985

public servant in Canada including appointment and service as High Commissioner to Ghana. Mr. Hart will take up his duties shortly and will be in touch with the companies concerned. We are today issuing a standard reporting format for the annual public reports which have been requested by the Government under the code of conduct.
Fourth, the Canadian Government will apply a voluntary ban on the sale of crude oil and refined products to South Africa. To this end, we are asking Canadian companies not to enter into any contracts for the sale and export of these goods to South Africa. Our sales in this area have been limited in the past. This measure is being taken now to ensure that Canada does not become an alternative source of supply in the future.
Fifth, we are bringing in an embargo on air transport between Canada and South Africa. It will cover both cargo and passenger flights. As we have no bilateral air agreement, neither country's airlines have obtained traffic rights from the other country for scheduled international services. Direct air transport between the two countries has, in consequence, been limited to occasional charters. The effect of this measure is therefore to stop those charter flights and to rule out reciprocal air service at least until the process of dismantling of apartheid is well engaged.
Sixth, a register has been opened for the voluntary measures which Canadian provinces and municipalities, as well as private institutions, organizations and firms have taken against apartheid. Thousands of Canadians have acted quietly on their own in protest and we encourage others to do so. Individuals and institutions which wish to do so are invited to register their actions by writing to me and indicating what they have done. The list of measures will have an exemplary impact and will be conveyed to the Secretary General of the United Nations in the expectation and with the recommandation that other nations might follow suit so that there will develop a world wide register of the actions of individuals who abhor apartheid.
Seventh, in view of the increasing number of arrests of non-violent opponents of apartheid, 1 am today announcing that an additional $1 million will be allocated on humanitarian grounds to assist the families of political prisoners and detainees in South Africa. These funds will be channelled through organizations such as the International Defence and Air Fund for Southern Africa and Canadian groups which are actively supporting the victims of apartheid.
In the prevailing circumstances, we must proceed with prudence and determination so that the words we say and the actions we take, alone or in concert with other countries, will help end injustice and violence. There have been some hopeful signs in recent days regarding the pass laws and common citizenship. We do not know whether the reforms hinted at will be realized but we certainly wish to encourage movement in that direction, and encourage the efforts of those South African business people who have long supported reform and who have now taken the initiative to encourage dialogue with the true representatives of blacks in South Africa.
Statements by Ministers
The days and weeks ahead will be marked on our side by a continued search for steps which may help to bring justice to South Africa and greater harmony to the region. For Canada that search will centre on consultations with our partners in Africa and elsewhere in the world, but particularly on the Commonwealth. Nor, of course, do we exclude talks with South Africa if the door remains open and we can influence events.
Seven of South Africa's close neighbours are Commonwealth countries and an eighth, Namibia, has been invited to join. Their people are closely linked. Their economies are deeply dependent on one another. Their security and their standing cannot be separated. There can be no peace in the region while South Africa remains at odds with its Commonwealth neighbours and while they live in fear of it. Apartheid is a Commonwealth problem. The question is not whether the Commonwealth has a role; by force of circumstance it must be concerned and involved. More than that, the Commonwealth has traditions and historic ties with South Africa which have prepared it to play a reconciling part if the Government of South Africa opens the door to it.
Despite the sharp differences which have divided Governments, the people of the Commonwealth and the people of South Africa are from the same traditions. There is a disposition to be hopeful and to seek reconciliation among South Africa's neighbours. What we must know is whether it will be reciprocated.
Another forum whose unanimous resolutions have consistently been ignored by the South African Government is the United Nations. At the imminent General Assembly, as it has in the past, Canada will encourage upon the world community the sort of concerted action which should leave South Africa with no doubts about the repugnance of its policies. As the world speaks, the unusual phenomenon of growing pressure on the South African Government from within that country will be given an opportunity to bear fruit. Our actions today, those taken by other Governments, and those actions which will be taken, will collectively keep the pressure on. If the Government of South Africa remains unbending to that pressure, then Canada will be left with no recourse other than to end our relations absolutely.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise in the House this morning to take part in this debate, but first I wish to congratulate the Minister on his presentation.

I think this statement is welcomed by this House and I-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
If there is a subject we should try to be very united on, it is the issue of apartheid in South Africa. We in

September 13, 1985
Statements by Ministers
this land know it is possible to overcome differences. We have come a long way down that road. Therefore, we should have absolutely no reservations about trying to make a positive contribution to make sure that every human being is equal around the globe. The situation in South Africa is a very good example of discrimination and domination which has to be strongly rejected. I am very glad that the Minister has come forward with this statement this morning because we need a comprehensive statement on this situation.
This past summer it appeared to be difficult for the Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to find common ground on this issue and I am happy to see that there now seems to be one position which is acceptable to everyone in your party and I am very pleased with that. The speech and all the remarks before the inauguration of sanctions were very good. But I think there is a big gap between the rhetoric and the reality. I wish the Minister had been able to get up in this Elouse and say that by, for example, January 1, 1986, we will sever our relations with South Africa if it does not act accordingly. This is because in analysing the situation in South Africa we realize that the moderates there are moving. It is not only on one side. The business community is now taking some positive steps to put pressure on the administration there and I think that economic sanctions are the answer. Some people feel that Canada has played a small part in the economy of South Africa. But, on the other hand, if every nation moves strongly and rapidly, the Government of South Africa will have no choice but to move. That is why I think the speech, the rhetoric, is very good but I am a bit disappointed that the Minister could not impose sanctions or give orders to certain people in Canada, many of whom we can give orders to, not to do business with South Africa. Of course, many of the banks have already stated their position that they will not lend South Africa any more money. But the problem is that we have to create a strong impression and thus my difficulty is with the actions of the Government. I think it might be seen by some as effective as mandatory sanctions; I agree with the Minister on that. But we see the debate in the United States where the President made a statement on apartheid which included somewhat less than the expected sanctions proposed in the Senate which is dominated by the Republicans. We saw what the EEC did this week. They put in place mandatory sanctions against South Africa.
So I feel the action is somewhat weak, but I do not want to be partisan and difficult about it. I just hope this will work. But we have to make clear that my such and such a date we will impose mandatory sanctions against South Africa in every field. I am glad to see that the Minister is even threatening to sever our relations with South Africa because that is what I wish we would do, to be very clear if thiings do not change very dramatically. Sometimes, when we are trying to find our way, we give a very confusing image of Canada, as happened this past summer. Our ambassador was recalled but the explanation given was that it was not quite a normal recall but that he was just recalled for consultation. I should have been made very clear that we had recalled him to give him new instructions or even to keep him here. But we did not do that. We waffled. We waffled as well between the statement of the Minister and that of the Prime Minister. Now it seems that there is cohesion in the Government and I think we are happy to support that.
The Speech is perfect but the action is weak. I hope the Minister will take the opportunity when it arises to set the date and say precisely what the action will be. Of course, one might argue that it will not have a big effect because the economic relations between Canada and South Africa are limited to something like S400 million in trade. That will not kill them. But if all nations of the world do the same thing we will succeed and there will be more justice in that country. There are political prisoners there just because they have expressed a political view. I am glad they have been named and the Minister is offering some help for their families and so on. We welcome that. But we have to keep the pressure on and encourage a dialogue between the moderates and the Government in South Africa to start soon.
There is a solution to these problems. Of course, some people are preoccupied with the fact that some of their privileges will disappear. But what is important is to give all the fundamental rights to the black people and 1 know and you know that when they are equal and first-class citizens of that land they will want the country to progress. 1 think humanity will be better off for that. So we welcome this move by the Minister in the sense that it shows cohesion in the Government against apartheid.
I think the action could have been stronger, and I hope it will not be seen that we are waffling somewhat. It would have been easy to say that these sanctions have to be followed rather than making them voluntary. The result may not have been different, but the speech would have been stronger and more influential. We have made some progress in that businesses and citizens have decided to use the peaceful tools they have of putting economic pressure on the business community. If the nations of the world were to do that from the other side, progress would be made. It is a step in the right direction. We must be as united as possible in that policy in Canada because, even though we are small and humble, we have had some experience of that nature in this land. We have proved that there is much generosity in human beings. This world problem presents an occasion to display that generosity. I welcome the statement and I hope that the Minister will tell South Africa exactly what we will do on January 1, 1986 if they do not move. I hope he will keep pressure on the Government to ensure that political prisoners will be freed as quickly as possible.
By doing so, Mr. Speaker, we could have made our contribution, because Canada is a country that could play an important role, considering the fact that as a country, we have shown it is possible to accommodate the differences that exist within a nation, and while giving all citizens a chance to be equal and
September 13, 1985

to keep their differences, their cultures and their language, to accept people of a different colour as equals and invite them to share in the benefits and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
Mr. Speaker, if they want to do the same thing in South Africa, I am confident that blacks and Asians and whites can live together, with a measure of good will, while respecting each others differences, and join in building a society that is truly worthy of the modern world.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, too, welcome the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) today. I am very pleased that he is continuing to influence and develop the Government's South Africa policy. The development has been slow, contradictory, and not enough but I, and I am sure many others, welcome the Minister's efforts.
For decades we in this Party have called for an end to the apartheid regime in South Africa. We have called for active Canadian and international efforts to end apartheid and bring about majority rule in that country. We urged the previous Liberal Governments to end Canada's de facto support for the regime in Pretoria through government assisted exports and traditional "quiet diplomacy". Despite continuing racism, repression and murder, and the ever-mounting international pressure for the isolation of South Africa, the Liberals did not act. Although the Hon. Minister says they would act today, they did not act over 20 years.
Once again, recent events in South Africa have caused widespread shock and revulsion in the international community and in Canada. Since the killings at Uitenhage on the 25th anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre, it has been a bloody year for South Africans. The unacceptable use of repression, force and murder by the state has been met in South African by resistance and abroad by revulsion and shock. No Government which must rely on such savage methods can make a claim to legitimacy among nations or support from its own people.
As Nelson Mandela said more than two decades ago, "Naked force and violence is the weapon openly used by the South African Government to beat down the struggles of the African people and to suppress their aspirations". What more evidence do we need than that only last night, more than two decades later, seven more blacks were killed. The brutal use of violence by a police state will ultimately lead to the defeat of those who employ such violence.
As the Minister has pointed out, the apartheid regime of South Africa now sits condemned, as it should have long ago, by international public opinion, by the family of nations, and by the inevitable course of history. The world and the majority of people in South Africa demand an end to apartheid. It is an unreformable evil that changes to citizenship regulations and pass laws will not correct. It is founded on racism and enforced by violence. Its "reform" will come only through the establishment of majority rule.
Statements by Ministers
New efforts and energies must be directed to the struggle for liberation and human decency in South Africa. While the Minister's statement is most welcome, it does not sufficiently represent the kind of new efforts which must be undertaken by Canada and other countries. In his statement the Minister said that in focusing our anger and applying steady pressure for change we must have the best information and judgments we can get on how to use our influence most effectively.
Nelson Mandela, in prison for 20 years or more, says that Governments must impose full economic sanctions. That is his judgment. The judgment of Desmond Tutu is the same. Seventy-three to 77 per cent of the black African population has said the same. That is their judgment on how to use our influence most effectively. In fact, other Canadians have taken as many, and sometimes more, initiatives until now than has the federal Government. Seven provincial Governments have established some economic sanctions by banning South African liquor sales. In fact, the Premier of Quebec has charged that the federal Government has lobbied the provinces not to take such actions. Trade unions in Canada have called for economic sanctions and the labour movement has refused to handle South African cargo at Vancouver. Petro-Canada has banned its latest sulphur shipment to South Africa, once again running ahead of External Affairs which has asked "to be kept up to date" on such initiatives. Even the Conservative Party leader in Manitoba has called for Canada to sever all economic relations with South Africa.
The Government has an obligation to undertake efforts and initiatives at least equal to those being undertaken by the people of Canada. In our view the Government should initiate a program of staged economic sanctions to be implemented within specific time limits in the absence of the dismantling of apartheid and concrete moves toward majority rule. As 1 have noted, South African blacks themselves are calling for such sanctions.
Canada should also actively promote at the United Nations broader international trade sanctions. There should be a tough mandatory rather than voluntary code of conduct, for Canadian business now operating in South Africa, and a government ban on any further Canadian investment in that country.
I welcome the Minister's call for the release of all political prisoners and detainees, especially ANC and UDF leaders. I urge him to consider Canadian financial assistance to the legal defence of such prisoners and the granting of charitable tax status for Canadian-based organizations providing such legal support. The Minister might also now consider something which the previous Government refused to do, namely matching funds raised in Canada by the Canadian Aid for South African Refugees Organization through CIDA. We have asked for this for a number of years. However, it has never been granted.
Perhaps the Minister would consider providing matching funds to aid South African refugees as we have matching funds in other parts of the world to aid refugees.

September 13, 1985
Petitions
Next, Canada must firmly renounce the illegal South African occupation of Namibia, in defiance of the United Nations and the work of the Western Contact Group. If Canada is to remain a member of that group it must work more rigorously for speedy South African withdrawal and a settlement that will include the active participation of SWAPO.
Finally, Canada must undertake special development assistance and support for states neighbouring South Africa to end their vulnerability to South African attack and their dependence on the South African economy.
Change will come to South Africa. It will either continue to be bloody and revolutionary, brought about by continued state repression and violence, or it will be peaceful orderly change through the speedy dismantling of apartheid and the establishment of majority rule.
The further measures announced by the Minister today, while most welcome, are largely voluntary. Canada can act now. Only by taking the lead in the community of nations in the imposition of economic sanctions-staged economic sanctions as we have said-within publicly stated time limits can other nations be influenced to take similar actions and can fundamental change become hopefully a reality in South Africa.

subtopic: PAROLE ACT, PENITENTIARY ACT, PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT, AND CRIMINAL CODE MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to rise to resume debate on this very important piece of
6594

September 13, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
legislation. At the conclusion of my remarks yesterday, I was raising the serious concern that this Bill, far from promoting public safety, will in fact have the opposite effect. I say that for a number of reasons. I know that my time is limited, but in the remaining time I certainly hope to be able to talk about some of the alternatives that we in the New Democratic Party feel are of significance and importance in this area.
I wish to turn to some of the specific concerns with Bill C-67, particularly when contrasted with some of the other similar Bills which have been before the House in the past. First, in dealing with the provisions which would close the so-called revolving door, I suggest the Bill has a rather bizarre provision which would, in fact, have a serious adverse impact on the community and on prisoners. What is stated in the Bill is that those prisoners who are initially convicted of crimes of violence, assault or homicide will not be eligible for remission on their mandatory supervision after one revocation. In other words, if there is any form of forfeiture of their mandatory supervision after they are out, they lose any opportunity for further earned remission. Not only will that add to overcrowding, it will cause serious problems within institutions because there are no incentives whatsoever for the prisoner to be of good behaviour. The one possible incentive which now exists is the possibility of earned remission, and that will be removed.
In addition, there is a glaring inconsistency in this Bill. I would ask Members of the House to consider the following situation. An inmate who is originally imprisoned for a nonviolent crime, for example, a fraud, is released from prison after two-thirds of his sentence has been served, because of his good behaviour, and is out on mandatory supervision. He is out on mandatory supervision for a couple of months and commits a serious crime of violence. Under the terms of this Bill, that prisoner would be returned to prison, having his mandatory supervision revoked, but would then be eligible for earned remission once he is back in. However, another prisoner, who was originally imprisoned for a crime of violence, in the same situation, is released after two-thirds of his sentence has been served, is out on the street and then has his mandatory supervision revoked, not because he commits a new crime but because he moves, is drunk or in breach of one of the other conditions, for example, he incurs a debt he is not supposed to incur. That individual will be hauled back into prison and forced to serve the remainder of his time in prison without any opportunity for earned remission.
What kind of ludicrous set-up is it when there are two individuals, both of whom are out on mandatory supervision, one of whom commits a serious crime of violence and is eligible for earned remission, and the individual whose mandatory supervision is revoked because he breaches a term or condition of mandatory supervision has the prison doors slammed shut until the end of his sentence? That is what this Bill does. It is just one of the many flaws in the Bill.
I wish to deal with another concern respecting this part of the Bill as well, that is to say, mandatory supervision can be revoked for any breach of any term or condition which is set out under the provisions of the Bill. That does not just mean a
future criminal offence. That can mean a breach of any of the conditions. Even the previous Government recognized that it was wrong to suggest that an individual, whose mandatory supervision is revoked for breach of a condition which is not a criminal offence, should be subject to loss of any future earned remission. That was wrong and that would be destructive of the environment within prisons, let alone to the question of fairness to the individual involved.
I would like to give one example of what that can lead to. A young man named Henry MacDonald, who was 30 years old, was released in September of 1980 on mandatory supervision. He had served two thirds of his sentence. One month later, however, the parole board revoked his release because he refused to live where he was told to live. He was told to live in London, Ontario and he left there and went home to his family in Brantford, Ontario. His family and even the local police said that he was causing no trouble whatsoever but he was in breach of that condition. So he was picked up and put back into prison in Millhaven Institution, the most violent maximum security institution in Canada. And that was done because he moved back with his family. On November 24, 1980, he was found stabbed to death in his cell.
This Bill will promote that kind of violence in our prison system and ultimately this Bill will promote increased violence in our communities. Serious questions have been raised with respect to the efficacy of the mandatory supervision program itself. This program, which was initially implemented in 1970 in fact has been shown to have virtually no impact whatsoever on the rate of recidivism of individuals who are subject to mandatory supervision. If one takes an individual who is on parole and another individual who is subject to mandatory supervision, the rate of involvement in future crime may be somewhat higher for the individual on mandatory supervision, but that is not surprising given the fact that it is the best risks who are originally given parole. If one takes two other groups of individuals, one group released after serving two thirds of their sentence and then serving the remainder without any form of mandatory supervision, and the second group who are released and are required to serve the remainder of their sentences under mandatory supervision, one finds there is no effect whatsoever on recidivism.
It has been argued by many that compulsory parole supervision in the community has no effect on the likelihood of an offender's reconviction. In fact, it causes serious problems. Really it is a form of surveillance, not a form of assistance and rehabilitation.
There are other problems with this Bill. I mentioned this bizarre provision whereby there is a double standard relating to the individual who is eligible for mandatory remission, on the one hand, and one who is not eligible for it, on the other hand, based solely on the offence for which they were originally incarcerated. But one of the most serious concerns I have about this Bill is the test which is applied to determine whether or not an individual will in effect be gated. As I indicated
September 13, 1985

yesterday, it has been shown to be virtually impossible to predict future violence. But under the terms of this Bill, the test is so broad and so sweeping that virtually anyone could be gated without any form of judicial review whatsoever. Let us bear in mind the fact, Mr. Speaker, that it is the same body which is determining that individual's eligibility for release that has previously been denying him that release all along the way. So we have the National Parole Board which is saying, "No, we are not going to grant you day parole. No, we are not going to grant you full parole", all the way along. Now it is suddently given an opportunity, after two thirds of the sentence has been served, to keep that person in. Do you think it is not going to take advantage of that, Mr. Speaker? Of course, it will. And on what grounds? Because of the possibility that he may be dangerous in the community, and that is decided without any real certainty or statistical basis for showing that we can predict that kind of violent behaviour.
At least, Mr. Speaker, in two other previous Bills, the criteria were more tightly drawn. In fact, I believe they related to the dangerous offender criteria in the Criminal Code. As it stands now, this new Bill would be directed not at inmates who have committed a serious personal injury offence as defined in the dangerous offender provisions of the Code, but it would be directed at a whole series of other offences which are going to be mentioned in a new schedule to the Parole Act. There will be 14 different offences. So it broadens the net very substantially.
With respect to the provision on the so-called "revolving door" syndrome; in that particular case, those individuals, having has their mandatory supervision revoked, will not even be eligible for discretionary parole in the future. The door will be permanently shut. So the criteria are far too broad.
As well, Mr. Speaker, I would note that under the previous Bill there was a requirement that psychiatric evidence be heard. One would have thought that it would be pretty essential in dealing with the possibility of future violence. Under this Bill, there is not even a requirement that there be any evidence heard from psychiatrists.
As well, Mr. Speaker, there are a number other concerns. I mentioned that the criteria are very broad. Effectively, the Board will now have to be satisfied of the likelihood of the commission of an offence causing death or serious harm and the guidelines can be established by the Governor in Council. I mentioned as well, Mr. Speaker, the fact that an individual who is detained pursuant to this provision, who is gated pursuant to this provision and is ordered to be detained in penitentiary, will not be eligible for parole. So if he is not eligible for parole, Mr. Speaker, then the fact is that another element of fairness in the procedure is denied to the prisoner. The final area I would like to touch on is that there is no sunset clause whatsoever in the gating provisions which are put forward by this Minister.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have serious concerns both with respect to the revolving door element of this Bill and with respect to the so-called gating provisions. What are the alternatives? I believe it is incumbent upon those of us who argue
Criminal Code Amendments
that this approach is the wrong approach to provide alternatives. I intend to do that in the few minutes which remain. First, I will note that in 1977, a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs issued a unanimous report to this House. The most important recommendation which was made was that we have to start to recognize that far too many Canadians who are convicted of crimes are imprisoned. Prisons should be used as a last resort and should be used only in those circumstances in which there is no other meaningful alternative and where the individual does pose a genuine threat to the community. The sentences in Canada are far too long in many cases. We are not looking at alternatives to imprisonment. Not only that, but we must go back even before that time, because if we are serious about reducing the level of crime in our communities and if we are serious about reducing prison population in Canada, we have to start looking at the prevention of crime. It is not good enough for us to focus slavishly on crime itself and on prisons. It is about time we in this country became serious about looking at the causes of crime and ways of preventing crime.
Many studies have been done-and we do not need any more studies-showing the kinds of action which should be taken to prevent crime, whether that be community-based alternatives, a recognition that in too many cases poverty and crime are inextricably linked, or a recognition of the fact that programs to deal with abuse, sexual abuse and other forms of violence against young people, are completely lacking in our society. These young people who have themselves been involved in this kind of abuse get involved in violent crime. What about programs for detection of learning disabilities? One estimate indicates as many as 80 per cent of the prison population have learning disabilities. What are we doing to try and prevent those individuals from being involved in crime at an early age? Nothing, absolutely nothing. We have to look at far more effective allocation of our resources to deal with young people in conflict with the law. As it stands now, in too many cases we ignore the concerns of young people. If we as a community made more effort to deal with young people in conflict with the law, hopefully that would result in less crime at later stages.
For those who are incarcerated we have to recognize there are programs which can and should be used for rehabilitation. One program which was strongly recommended by the subcommittee and ignored by the previous Government and this Government is that of work. Is it such a revolutionary thing to suggest that prisoners in Canadian prisons should be working? That was one of the essential recommendations of the subcommittee report. Let us put prisoners to work, meaningful work, within the system. Not only will that assist us in rehabilitation, it will cut down significantly on the cost of prisons. This Government is concerned about the deficit, as we all are, so I would have thought that it would want to look at that recommendation for a national prison industry's corporation. But no, what does it do? It brings in a Bill which will increase the cost of our prison system and add to the overcrowding.

Criminal Code Amendments
What about those prisoners in the system? I mentioned the importance of work. There are far too many in the system who are not working. For those who may be sex offenders, instead of dealing with meaningful programs to try and rehabilitate those individuals, what is this Government doing? It is cutting funds for programs for sex offenders in the federal prison system. The sex offender treatment program in Campbell River, British Columbia, was treating 12 people. It was very cost effective and reduced the likelihood of further offences. What happened to that program? It was axed by the Government. Therefore, when this Government talks about the safety of our communities on the one hand and on the other eliminates programs which seek to rehabilitate sex offenders, it is speaking out of both sides of its mouth and we in this Party reject that kind of approach. I have mentioned the problems of overcrowding in our prison system. I have mentioned the problems of arbitrary actions which give rise to frustration. These are things such as involuntary transfers, plucking an individual from one prison in the middle of the night and taking him to another prison. This adds to the tension, frustration, overcrowding, double bunking and so on.
In concluding my remarks, the point I want to make on this important Bill is that it is not the answer. The Government is conning Canadians in suggesting that by taking this approach it will in any way reduce the level of violent crime in our communities. In fact, if this approach is adopted the opposite will be the effect. We have to get that message out very clearly. Sure, the chiefs of police are anxious to have this Bill adopted but we have to take a broader approach, one which reflects the concerns of our communities for their safety. We have to recognize our concerns about basic rights within the prison community as well. It is for that reason we in the NDP reject this approach, and it is for that reason that my colleagues and I will be opposing this Bill and urging the Government to come to its senses and take meaningful steps to prevent crime. We have to introduce meaningful programs for rehabilitation within our prison system. Most important of all, we have to ensure that steps are taken to provide alternative to imprisonment so that our human warehouses, the prisons of today, will not cost us that much money and a program which has failed miserably will no longer burden Canadian citizens.

subtopic: PAROLE ACT, PENITENTIARY ACT, PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT, AND CRIMINAL CODE MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this particular debate dealing with Bill C-67. I would like to indicate at the outset that we in the Liberal Party support this Bill. It is, for all intents and purposes, identical to that Bill which was introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) and former Solicitor General. Unlike the NDP, we in the Liberal Party are concerned first and foremost with innocent law-abiding Canadians. We have to ensure that the utmost protection is afforded to those in our society who live according to the rule of law. I want to cite a few examples to indicate
why we in the Liberal Party support this Bill. A year ago last July an individual released on mandatory supervision after serving 14 years for rape went out into the community and killed four people in Brandon, Manitoba. The corrections people had no choice, that individual had to be released. I would like to ask whether the lives of those four individuals could have been saved if this Bill had been law at that time? There are other examples where individuals released on mandatory supervision have gone out and committed some very serious crimes. Another example, one I am sure Hon. Members will recall, was last year when a Woodstock man, once again released on mandatory supervision, killed a police officer in the Montreal area and then killed a student. I ask again whether the lives of those two individuals could have been saved had this legislation been in place?
My friend, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) indicates that this Bill will do a profound injustice to prisoners and those who are serving sentences in the community. The NDP have often claimed that they support the ordinary Canadian. Listening to the Hon. Member, one has to ask who the NDP is representing given their position on this particular Bill. Are they concerned about the safety of the public or are they advocates for the inmates? We, too, in the Liberal Party are concerned about rehabilitation. We are concerned about those who are serving sentences in our prisons. However, our primary concern is the safety of those citizens who live their lives according to the rule of law. This Bill is necessary and important. There are those of us in the Liberal Opposition who believe that other steps have to be taken to ensure the utmost safety for our citizens and I was pleased to hear the Minister indicate that his Department and the Department of Justice are continuing to monitor the situation and continuing to think of new proposals to ensure the utmost protection for society.
Now, what is mandatory supervision? The Minister and the Hon. Member for Burnaby explained what it was. However, I suspect that a lot of Canadians do not understand what it really means. I have to admit, as a lawyer and as a new Member of Parliament, I really did not know the distinction between mandatory supervision and parole. Parole, in my view, is far more successful than mandatory supervision. As Hon. Members know, most inmates become eligible for full parole after serving one-third of their sentences. An exception are those who are serving life sentences. Inmates are eligible for day parole after serving one-sixth of their sentence. The National Parole Board considers each individual case, the crime the individual committed, and the prisoner's behaviour while serving his sentence, and determines whether an inmate can be released without being a threat to the lives of innocent people. For the most part our parole system is good because the Parole Board has discretion. It decides whether or not to release a particular inmate. Statistics indicate that 74 per cent of parolees are successful and that only a small percentage of those released on parole are eventually returned to institutions.
What is the case with mandatory supervision? In 1970 the concept of mandatory supervision was introduced. Prior to that
September 13, 1985

time there existed statutory remission through which the sentence of an inmate was reduced by operation of law. Under statutory remission an individual would serve his time in jail and then have no period of supervision in the community. Once the inmate had served his sentence he was thrown out into the community. It was widely thought that that was not fair to society or to the inmate. It was thought to be necessary to have some form of supervision, so we experimented with mandatory supervision. Under mandatory supervision inmates accumulate remission which is known as earned remission. For every month they serve in a federal penitentiary they get 15 days off for good behaviour. That resulted in the elimination of one-third of the inmate's sentence. The problem is that that inmate would automatically be released, notwithstanding the crimes he had committed or the threat he may present to the community. The authorities had no option other than to release that individual into the community.
We have heard horror stories about individuals who were released on mandatory supervision. I referred to the case of the individual in Brandon, Manitoba who killed four individuals, and to the man from Woodstock. These are the worst of the worst criminals. Those model inmates who have shown a sincere desire to rehabilitate themselves and have shown that they can live a law-abiding life are eligible for day parole after serving one-sixth of their sentence and for full parole after serving one-third of their sentence. The model inmates become eligible for parole. Those who are released on mandatory supervision are the inmates for which the authorities have refused parole. The authorities have concluded that these inmates should not be released, but because of mandatory supervision they were forced to release them. Attempts were made to reincarcerate some of these individuals and we had the problem of gating which was an attempt to reincarcerate those inmates who posed a very serious threat to the community. It became apparent over a period of time that mandatory supervision was not working.
I would like to cite some statistics which would corroborate that contention. The Solicitor General's Department undertook a study of mandatory supervision. The study is entitled Mandatory Supervision: A Discussion Paper. It is a report of the Committee on Mandatory Supervision which was released and tabled in early 1981. The statistics relating to inmates who were released on mandatory supervision between January 1975 and December 1979 are somewhat shocking. In that period of time individuals who were released on mandatory supervision committed 52 homicides, 31 murders, and 21 offences of manslaughter. Does the Hon. Member for Burnaby and the rest of the New Democratic Party think that if this Bill had been in force some of these lives could have been saved? It will be argued that crime is inevitable and that if these individuals were not kept incarcerated there would be no way to stop them from committing murders and other offences.
In that same period of time statistics show that inmates released on parole committed nine murders and nine offences of manslaughter. There were no cases of attempted murder by those released on parole while there were 11 such offences
Criminal Code Amendments
committed by individuals released on mandatory supervision. Ten individuals released on parole were convicted of rape while 25 inmates released under mandatory supervision were convicted of that crime. The list goes on. Four individuals released under the parole system were convicted of sexual assault while 23 individuals released under mandatory supervision were convicted of that crime. Seventeen individuals released under parole were convicted of assault while 153 released under mandatory supervision were convicted of that crime. With regard to kidnapping the figures are 6 versus 15 and with regard to robberies they are 127 versus 394. Mr. Speaker, res ipsa loquitur, the facts speak for themselves.
This is a good Bill, Mr. Speaker, and the Liberal Party intends to support it, but we also recognize that it is only a first step and that other action must be taken to ensure that society is safe. When a convicted individual is given a sentence the public believes that that individual will serve that sentence. However if an individual is convicted of a serious crime and given a sentence of 12 years, we know that that individual will not necessarily serve that period of time. Under today's sentences, the individual will serve anywhere from one-third to the full warrant when the sentence has expired. Indeed, very few individuals serve their full sentences today. It is true that this Bill may result in certain inmates being kept in for their full warrant. Our concern with respect to this legislation is that there must be a period of supervision in the community. We simply cannot release an inmate outright after serving a lengthy prison term. It is not fair to the community and it is not fair to the individual. There must be a transition period. My friend, the Hon. Member for Burnaby laughs. I listened to the alternatives that he presented and I, on behalf of the Liberal Party, would like to make some suggestions.
He is suggesting that as part of that sentence there be a period of supervision during the duration of that sentence. If I understand the comments made by the Hon. Member, his Party supports the existing provisions with respect to mandatory supervision notwithstanding the statistics which clearly indicate that the concept is a failure to a certain degree.
1 will ask the committee to consider the possibility of reforming the sentencing procedure in Canada to include, at the end of a period of incarceration, a period of supervision required by law. For example, with respect to someone sentenced for a 12-year prison term and who is not released because that person is a threat to society, according to the legislation there would be a period of perhaps one to three years of supervision where the authorities can continue to exercise some control over the individual to ensure that that individual is able to begin living a normal life. That is an option that should be considered. Other options and alternatives should also be considered.
The previous Liberal administration was concerned about sentencing in Canada. I am sure Hon. Members will agree that a great percentage of Canadians believe that sentences are far too lenient. During this Parliament, Bill C-18 provided

September 13, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
for stiffer penalties with respect to drunk driving. That Bill too was introduced by the previous Liberal administration but died without becoming law. All Hon. Members, including those representing the New Democratic Party, supported that legislation because of the belief that Canadians wanted more severe penalties with respect to drunk drivers.
The previous administration was concerned about sentencing over-all in Canada with respect to the commission of criminal offences. Therefore, the previous administration established a commission-originally known as the Sinclair Commission-now known as the Archambault Commission. It is reviewing the whole sentencing procedure in Canada in order to determine whether sentences are appropriate in the circumstances for the various offences. It is determining what criteria and what principles ought to be used in sentencing.
We, as parliamentarians, have a duty to take into consideration the public view with respect to crime and sentencing. In some ways, the results of that commission will have to reflect a concern by the public that sentencing is too lenient.
The Liberal Party is also concerned about the population in our prisons. However, our paramount concern is the safety of the public. We believe that we must become more strict with violent offenders, those who commit offences against the persons by assault, rape, murder and manslaughter. It is with those individuals that we must become more severe and if it means spending more money to keep these individuals incarcerated when they pose a serious threat, so be it. We cannot put a value on human life. It is not possible to put a value on the lives of the four individuals who were murdered in Brandon, Manitoba by the inmate who was released on mandatory supervision. We cannot put a price on the 52 individuals who were killed by those released on mandatory supervision between 1975 and 1979. It is costly to keep people incarcerated and it is also costly to keep the public safe. If it comes to a question of spending more money or releasing violent offenders, we believe in spending the extra money to ensure the safety of our citizens.
Some people who are incarcerated should not be in prison. They are those who commit offences against property. One could argue that they should not be in our prisons and that sentences for those particular crimes whould be reduced and other methods of punishing these people should be used. Such punishment could include community service orders where these individuals could pay society back for their crime by working in the community or contributing in some other way to the community. We believe that other methods of punishment should be used for those individuals while maintaining the concept of deterrence and recognizing its importance in order to deter like minded people from committing similar crimes.
While we applaud the Government for looking for other ways to penalize those who breach the Criminal Code of Canada, we are concerned about the violent offenders. That is why we believe Bill C-67, while not the final step, is a tremendous step forward to ensure the safety of our citizenry.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby seems to be living in a cloud. He apparently suggests a utopia when talking about eliminating crime. While we can do much in an attempt to reduce the level of crime, my hon. friend seems to believe that by waving a magic wand or by using some magic potion, crime can be eliminated. However, we must accept the reality that crime in Canada will continue.
We are very fortunate in this country with respect to the level of crime and the safety of our citizens. One need only look south of the 49th parallel to realize how fortunate we are concerning crime. Our record of being one of the safest countries in the world is one of which we can be proud. How many people in the world can walk freely in their major urban areas without fear of being assaulted in any way? When we walk in downtown Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, it is reassuring to have a certain degree of confidence in our police force and a confidence that we are safe. However, that is not the case in Detroit, New York and many other major cities not only in the United States but throughout the world.
We should count our blessings that we do have a very safe country. However, that does not mean that we can stop there. We can make it safer by ensuring that those individuals who show a clear risk of violent conduct and pose that threat to society will be kept incarcerated.
As the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) indicated, it costs approximately $40,000 a year to keep an inmate in a federal institution. It costs over $100,000 to construct one new prison cell. Although it is costly, I repeat that the money is well spent when ensuring the safety of the public.
This legislation, Mr. Speaker, will give the National Parole Board discretion that it did not have with respect to mandatory supervision. In many ways the National Parole Board will have the discretion it has under the parole system. I would like to reiterate that those candidates eligible for mandatory supervision are not model prisoners or those serving time for property offences. We are talking about the rapists, those who have committed serious assaults and we are talking about federal, not provincial inmates. All inmates in federal penitentiaries are serving at least a two-year sentence. These are the most serious offenders. The less serious offenders are dealt with in provincial institutions. Any inmate serving less than two years serves the sentence in a provincial institution.
This Bill will give discretion to the National Parole Board and it will establish criteria and procedures to retain in custody until warrant expiry, or place under strict residential conditions those inmates considered to pose a clear risk of violent conduct beyond a release date that would have been established by earned remission.
I took the liberty of calling some of those who adjudicate these particular cases from the National Parole Board. I took the liberty to call other experts in the field to ask their opinion with respect to this legislation. The overwhelming majority of those to whom I spoke considered this Bill a step forward and
September 13, 1985

considered any move to give the National Parole Board more discretion as a positive step toward creating a safer society.
