We will listen to those groups. Yes, I have spoken to Claire Culhane and I have spoken to inmates. As the critic for the Solicitor General in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, I have listened to inmates and I have spoken to them. I have also spoken to victims. As a lawyer I have acted for victims. I have been concerned with the level of violent crime. 1 commit myself and my Party to doing everything we possibly can to make our society safer. When we look at this Bill, we do not say that it will do a profound injustice to prisoners, but we in the Liberal Party say that if Members do not pass this Bill, and if they do not support it, they will be doing a profound injustice to the people they represent as parliamentarians. Members will be doing a profound injustice to the thousands and millions of Canadians who live a law-abiding life. I ask the Hon. Member and the NDP, who are they representing? Are
Criminal Code Amendments
they representing their constituents, or are they representing a very narrow interest group, as they so often do?
Getting back to the legislation, Mr. Speaker, it will allow inmates convicted of violent offences specified by the criteria one chance for release on mandatory supervision. As 1 indicated earlier, this will eliminate the revolving door syndrome. It is fair to give an inmate one chance. First, that inmate has to convince the National Parole Board that he or she ought to be released because the individual is not a threat to society. After having convinced the Parole Board of that, if the inmate breaches a condition of supervision or commits a further offence and is convicted of a further offence, then surely no one can argue that the individual be given another chance. That aspect of the Bill is a very substantial step forward.
The Bill would also establish procedural safeguards and criteria that would limit the application of the measures to only the most dangerous offenders. I am sure Hon. Members have reviewed the legislation and realized the offenders that we are dealing with in this legislation are offenders who are serving time in jail for manslaughter, attempted murder, causing bodily harm with intent, assault with a weapon or causing bodily harm, aggravated assault, assaulting a police officer, sexual assault, including rape, et cetera. These are the individuals serving more than two years. They are the ones who have to be watched and who will be looked at. This legislation does not deal with those individuals serving time in federal penitentiaries for offences against property, for example. I think it is only reasonable we look at those who have committed serious offences to determine, using certain criteria, whether there is any likelihood or risk that they might go out into society and commit another serious offence. 1 think that is only reasonable, Mr. Speaker.
The Parole Board will first look at those individuals who have been denied parole. It will then make a determination whether reasonable grounds exist to conclude whether a person is likely to commit, prior to the expiry of his or her sentence, a violent crime that will result in harm. There are those who would argue the standard is not high enough, that reasonable grounds give the National Parole Board too much discretion. There are those who would argue that the standard is too low and that there should be a stricter standard as to when certain individuals should be kept in custody under a detention order.
There are those who argue that the onus should be on an inmate to show to the authorities, the National Parole Board, that they are likely candidates to be released and that they are not a threat to society. Under the legislation, it is up to the National Parole Board. There is a presumption that an individual after having committed a serious crime will be release after serving two-thirds of the sentence. There is a presumption in the law as it reads that that individual is to be released and the onus is on the National Parole Board or the authorities to apply the criteria and determine whether the individual should be kept in custody. Indeed, there are those people who argue that the onus should be on the accused and that the presumption should be that all inmates serve their full sentences because under the Criminal Code, if one commits a

September 13, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
particular crime, one can be sentenced up to a particular time in prison. There are those people who argue that a 12-year sentence means a 12-year sentence and that in some ways our federal statutes conflict. The Criminal Code indicates, for example, that one is to serve 12 years, yet other legislation indicates that if one earns a remission, then the 12-year sentence is no longer a 12-year sentence but an 8-year one. The proposed legislation will give that discretion to the National Parole Board.
The legislation goes on to indicate that even if an inmate does not meet the criteria with respect to the offences listed in the schedule to the Bill and if the Commissioner of Corrections has reasonable grounds to believe that the inmate is likely to commit, prior to the expiry of the sentence, a violent crime which will result in violent harm, he may refer the case to the Chairman of the National Parole Board for a detention hearing. This particular provision might cause some concern. It provides that those who are not serving sentences for crimes against a person may be subjected to a detention hearing before the National Parole Board. There are also those people who have suggested that perhaps in those cases the person should not be detained.
There are safeguards with respect to the legislation. For example, the Parole Act will be amended to entitle all inmates to an annual review of a detention order. It does not mean that once the National Parole Board makes a decision with respect to a particular inmate that that is the end of the case and the inmate is required to serve his or her full sentence. An inmate who is refused release on mandatory supervision will have the legal right to have his or her case reconsidered every year. If there is a material change in circumstances and the particular individual is able to show to the National Parole Board and to the authorities that he or she does not pose a risk to society, the particular inmate may be permitted a release in the future. We consider this to be a good provision.
The legislation also provides that three members of the board must be present when a detention hearing is held. We consider that to be a good feature as well. Three responsible individuals would be reviewing a particular case as opposed to a single individual, and that provides the system with a degree of more fairness. The National Parole Board is not only given the discretion to release a particular inmate, but it could also attach conditions to a particular release. That is also a good feature of the legislation. We need to have confidence that members of the National Parole Board will act reasonably and according to the best interests of society first and the particular inmate second.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby indicated in his submission that the legislation in some way will increase violent crime. I was somewhat surprised when I heard him indicate that that was the position of the New Democratic Party. He called upon the Official Opposition to provide the names of groups which have spoken to our Party. I note that my time is coming to an end, but in conclusion I would like to challenge the Hon.
Member for Burnaby and the New Democratic Party to provide facts with respect to their submission that more violence will occur. If the NDP took the time to read the report published by the Department of the Solicitor General, they may arrive at a different conclusion. I reiterate that the Official Opposition supports the Bill in principle. We welcome a full and complete discussion of it when it is before the legislative committee. We invite all interested groups and parties to appear before the legislative committee to put forward their submissions. If we approach the Bill in a reasonable way, I am sure Canadians can rest assured that we have done everything we possibly can as parliamentarians to ensure the safety of law-abiding citizens.

subtopic: PAROLE ACT, PENITENTIARY ACT, PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT, AND CRIMINAL CODE MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this Bill. I do not think I can let the remarks of the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) just go by without passing comment. I think they were almost too intellectually dishonest and at times demonstrated a dangerous diversion from the principles of British and Canadian common law. His proposal for those who were sentenced by the courts to serve their full sentences and to have the Canadian penitentiary system, the police and courts tack on surveillance in the communities afterward is a very dangerous proposal which is not operative anywhere in the western world. Perhaps the Hon. Member might want to name a few police states where it occurs, but I am certainly unaware of any precedent or anyone associated with the criminal justice system who has ever proposed or supported such an intellectually dishonest and naive proposal.
I came to this House having been elected as a Member of Parliament from being a corrections officer, I have some relevant experience to lay before the House in relation to these proposals. I have had discussions with almost all my colleagues in the field, whether they be jail guards, national parole officers, probation officers in the provinces, prosecutors or police, regarding this kind of proposal for more than a decade. I must say that this approach is tragically narrow and will prove to be both dangerous and expensive. I will demonstrate in my remarks this afternoon the reason for that. I hope those Members of Cabinet who are here will pass on my views to the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) in the hopes that he will change the approach in this Bill.
As was demonstrated by the previous speaker, there is a real need for the House to inform itself fully of the penal and parole system in Canada before tinkering with it. For the Liberal Party to put up someone today who admitted before speaking that he did not even know what mandatory supervision was, demonstrates the lack of depth in that Party and why, for more than a decade, the very activities which he quoted were occurring. Whether it was the tragic murders in Brandon, Manitoba or elsewhere, that Government never responded to such activities in any meaningful way within the system of corrections that exists in Canada today. We have one of the highest rates of incarceration in the western world and, by a long shot, one of the most expensive.
September 13, 1985

I think we should deal with facts. Some very excellent evidence was given by the Canadian Criminal Lawyers' Association before the Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs of the Senate less than two years ago. I should like to refer to the evidence of two very knowledgeable persons in this field, Mr. David Cole and Professor Allan Manson of Queen's University. Speaking about the basic parameters contained in the Bill, I should like to quote from Mr. Cole's evidence:
It is our respectful submission that it is dangerous to tinker with one element of an integrated system because to do so creates new tensions, exacerbates pressures and raises unforeseen problems elsewhere in the system.
It is our submission that any response to violent offenders and recidivists which expects to be ameliorative must flow from a full and open inquiry which will permit Parliament to generate an appropriate systematic response based on a clear understanding and accurate perceptions.
Much like the Bill on prostitution with which we dealt on Monday, we are seeing the House charging down the road dealing with a very sensitive public issue. No one in this House wants a corrections or court system operating in which Parliament knowingly allows dangerous offenders to become involved in unpredictable activities in our communities. To a certain extent, this Bill will allow that to happen and I will demonstrate that.
Very much like the prostitution Bill with which we dealt on Monday, this Bill deals with a symptom of a very serious and chronic sociological disease that is systemic not only in our society but in every society that has existed since we began to organize ourselves some 4,000 or 5,000 years ago. This is a very complex issue and what is being proposed in the Bill before us today is tantamount to amputating a limb when a bone is broken and in fact requires a cast.
We can debate this afternoon and in committee ad nauseam the intentions of incarceration, punishment and the removal of freedom from men and women who are placed in institutions in order to protect society or whatever. However, we must understand that all inmates eventually return to live among us. This Bill and, I believe, the remarks of the previous speaker, demonstrate an incredible naivety about what actually happens, particularly within the maximum security institutions of this country. To claim that keeping someone who is serving a 10-year sentence incarcerated for the full 10 years makes him somehow safer when going back into the community than does releasing him after seven years with some kind of professional supervision from a parole officer and a federal system is incredibly naive. I predict that this will create a hot box situation.
I have spoken to jail guards, wardens and national parole officers. From having worked within the system, I have some understanding of what it means when we begin to hot box which is to say to tell an inmate that he is not getting out until the very last day. There is then no opportunity for any give and take within the institution. There is no reason for an inmate to do what a guard asks or to follow the rules of the institution.
Criminal Code Amendments
When an inmates is released early and is under mandatory supervision, there are certain things that 1 as a professional in the field can do for him. For instance, if he is not supposed to be in a beer parlour, I could go into the beer parlour to find him and send him back. If he did not keep his job, was not turning up on time, was not making restitution or family payments or was not doing a whole host of other things, there was some kind of control over that under a caring albeit professional system. At least the people coming out of institutions knew that there was some supervision there.
It is naive of the previous speaker and the Solicitor General to be moving this Bill forward. Many Canadians will agree that if someone is given a 10-year sentence, he should serve a 10-year sentence. However, we as a Parliament must have some kind of responsibility to integrate the concepts of the penal system and the parole system with the court system because if not, individuals will be more dangerous when they come out the other end.
As the committee will discover, there have been very few studies made around the world to see whether or not there has been a dramatic increase in homicides or crimes of that sort after parole because those things are incredibly difficult to predict. The National Parole Board is aware that it will be forced to make all kinds of subjective decisions based upon things like an argument with a guard or an inmate flipping his dinner on the floor. It will have to make all kinds of subjective evaluations related to whether or not that individual will be dangerous if returned to the community.
We are not taking the kind of approach that we should be taking to ensure to the maximum potential the safety of the community. I spent a great many nights worrying about people who were on mandatory supervision and were not where they were supposed to be. 1 would go to incredible lengths to try to locate them before taking the ultimate step of placing them back in an institution. That opportunity will no longer exist. We are talking about the most dangerous group of individuals within our society, individuals who will be touched by this legislation.
I plead with Members of the House to slow down and apply logic to this matter. We should not even ask to have a whole bunch of studies done. We should think it through. Is it safe to tell someone who has taken another person's life that he will have to serve every day of his sentence and will then be booted out the door of a security institution? Is it safe to have that individual who has been locked up night and day, 24 hours a day, for 10 years put back on the street without having any kind of an integrated return to the community? Sheer logic tells us that that is not the case. If there is not some kind of professional surveillance, there will be failures for worse than the four homicides quoted by the Hon. Member of the Liberal Party. The House must be very careful in condoning this type of approach.
It may be easy for Members to say that we passed a piece of legislation indicating that people will serve all of their time, but I have looked at the statistics, Mr. Speaker. For a very short period of time, a number of people who have been

September 13, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
dangerous in the past will be backlogged within the penitentiary system in Canada, but a few years down the road, a heck of a lot more than would ordinarly be going onto the streets at one time will be put on the streets of Canada. Then we will see the blip on the screen. I think Canadians will be shocked to find that this Parliament on this day did not deal in a more decent way with the situation. When it comes to correctional law, today really is Friday the 13th.
There are two key issues at which we must look with great care because they are the key components outside of the expansion of the National Parole Board and a number of other rather superficial issues dealt with in this Bill. There are two revolving-door syndrome and gating. Members have touched upon these matters, but I think it is important to remind ourselves of what has become known within legal circles as the revolving-door syndrome. This is when prisoners on mandatory supervision have their supervision revoked and are then returned to prison, and after serving more time, they again come out on mandatory supervision, a supervision which is again revoked. Dealing with that seems to be the first objective of this Bill and I think it is worth putting on the record a paragraph from the evaluation of this proposal done by the Library of Parliament. I quote from Part II:
Inmates of federal penitentiaries earn remission of sentence under s.24 of the Penitentiary Act. (Remission is applicable to all sentences except those for which there is a minimum time which must be served before eligibility for release, e.g. murder.)
For every month of sentence (or portion thereof) during which "he has applied himself industriously ... to the program of the penitentiary in which he is imprisoned", an inmate is entitled to 15 days remission of sentence (or a fraction thereof, where time served is less than a month). If an inmate earns all possible remission he or she becomes eligible for release after having served two-thirds of his or her sentence. (Most inmates "earn" all possible remission, because it is virtually vested, subject to removal for bad behaviour, on the commencement of sentence.) Before 1970, an inmate who was released as a result of remission left the institution free and clear of supervision, and the possibility of having to return to serve the balance of his or her sentence. In that year, however, the mandatory supervision programme was introduced.
Inmates released by reason of remission were to be subjected to the same type of supervision as paroled inmates; and, accordingly, were also to be subject to revocation of release because of misbehaviour while under mandatory supervision. Section 15 of the Parole Act governs mandatory supervision; and subjection (2) (inmates who are conditionally released by reason of a decision of the National Parole Board, usually after having served one-third of their sentence) thereof direct that those provisions of the Act dealing with suspension and revocation of parole to mandatory supervision as if it were a parole release.
The second point which needs to be clarified for those Canadians who want to focus their attention on an issue that is important in society is the matter of gating. That gives vast powers to the National Parole Board to designate that certain individuals be denied mandatory supervision until their sentence is complete. On that matter, I quote again from the Library of Parliament study which has the following to say:
On the basis of s.16, inmates deemed dangerous would be nominally released, but would have that release suspended and revoked as they reached the prison gate-hence the appellation "gating". Thus, there would be a technical release, which it was thought would enable the Board to use s.16.
Gating was immediately challenged in court. In various courts, there was some division as to whether this use of s.16 was appropriate. The issue was resolved on May 17, 1983 when the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the view of two courts of appeal that s.16 could only be used when there is a genuine release of the
inmate, and that it could only be invoked to re-commit the inmate based on post-release conduct. In effect, an inmate had to be given a chance "on the street" before his release could be terminated for misconduct.
Having dealt with the two key components, I think we have to look carefully at what type of image the new Government is attempting to create out there. There is no doubt that there is a real mood among many Canadians who have friends, family or someone who has been victimized by someone either on parole or mandatory supervision. I think it is responsible of the Government to respond; however, not to respond in a way which will create a more dangerous situation in the near future. It creates an image of law and order for many Canadians which, in fact, is just not the case. A government which will keep those convicted for every day of their sentence given by a court creates the image of safety. That is an illusion because, in fact, it increases the likelihood of dangerous behaviour from someone who is kept without any possibility of an early release.
The hot box in the prison system is something we have to look at. I hope the committee will do this because we are all too well aware in this House that it costs, on average, $40,000 a year to keep an inmate on the inside in this country. We are all too well aware that it costs in excess of an eighth of a million dollars for every cell constructed. Community supervision by a probation or parole officer costs between $3,000 and $5,000 a year. This cost varies from province to province.
The parole service evolved to assist in the transition of inmates back into the community. For those paroled after having served roughly one-third of their sentence, or for those on mandatory supervision after having served roughly two-thirds of their sentence, it provided an opportunity for them to deal with someone, whether it was by phone, coming into an office or dealing on the job site. This person could assist. 1 think many Members forget that if someone has been incarcerated for five, ten or more years, the simplest things often become the most complicated. 1 am speaking of setting up bank accounts, turning up regularly to work, buying new clothes, things that are simple. When the released inmate runs into something that is difficult he often tends to be very short fused if, for example, he has been told on the job site that he needs to get a different type of boot, or something of that nature. Often he thinks he is being picked on. Without some type of bouncing board, released inmates tend to veer off into unusual behavioural patterns. The Hon. Member for Burnaby has pointed this out. He is one of the few people in the House who has done more in working toward real legislation which would have a real potential benefit to the safety of communities than anyone else in the House. The Hon. Member comes from a community where there are a substantial number of inmates because they are actually housed there. There are few Members in this House who are more aware of the need for good, accurate and penetrating legislation which really deals with the problem rather than this type of illusory legislaiton which is designed for hot lines and mail-outs. It is not designed to deal with the problem.
September 13, 1985

Rumours are also rife now in the national parole service that the next move is to privatize parole. This is something which has been done in the United States and which has not been very successful. If this is to be the trade mark of corrections moves by the new Government, I will not doubt for a moment that we will see the privatization of parole, in part, with the argument that the dangerous inmates are now being dealt with inside the prisons as opposed to on the street because they are serving full sentences. It will probably be argued also that measures such as the dangerous offenders provisions of the Criminal Code are getting them out of the way.
We heard the Liberal Member quoting statistics related to parole and mandatory supervision demonstrating, once again, a preposterous naivety of who it is within each of those components and what the background of the whole issue is. I would like to hear from the Minister in this respect. I am sorry to say that he is not in attendance, although I am pleased to see the former Solicitor General here, who I think has a real interest in this issue. I would like to hear him list who in this country among wardens, guards, parole officers, judges, criminologists, sociologists or community resource groups endorse this approach. The role of institutions for male and female offenders must change. When society, through Parliament, determines that a person should be removed for two or more years from society for the committing of an offence, society should also know that this House is running a sound corrections and rehabilitation operation. That is just not happening. In fact, many of those avenues will be precluded if this Bill is passed unamended. I am confident that for a majority of those incarcerated we can operate secure facilities based on user-pay, as was touched on by the Hon. Member for Burnaby. Why should we pay $40,000 per inmate per year, plus all court costs, family costs and restitution? We should be moving toward a system of reduced institutional violence by designing the operations to be productive, where inmates are involved to as high a degree as possible in producing the goods and capital costs of their own incarceration, restitution, court costs, and so on. Certainly, the prevention of crime, as touched on by the Hon. Member for Burnaby, is a crucial area we have to look at because the tendency in many provinces, certainly in British Columbia, is to cut back on those people who have all types of studies demonstrating that their work has prevented many people with learning disabilities, and so on, from getting into a life of crime.
I would like to finish by saying that the distinction of the historic role of parole in this country is an error of extreme proportions. My final example is that of a convicted killer serving 10 years with no mandatory supervision and no parole. The proposal being put forward by the Liberal Party is that that person should be dropped into society. I would tend to agree more with the new Solicitor General who does not propose the Liberal Draconian proposal which is without any court order, any kind of legal process, that people be placed under surveillance after the fact. Anyone who believes what the Liberal Member had to say is dreaming in Technicolor.
Criminal Code Amendments
We need changes to this Bill in the interests of Canadian public safety.	.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to respond to that question because I believe it is one of the most important things which we in this House and in committee are going to look at. I hope that the committee takes the time to hear submissions from wardens, guards and from groups associated with prisoners both on the inside and on the outside because it is going to "hot box" those institutions. That is a fairly common terminology for what occurs within the prison population when there are people who have nothing to gain by good behaviour. They have everything to gain in terms of control within the elements of the prison population by being what we could call "bad actors". If we had someone serving a 10, 15 or 20-year sentence who does not stand to gain any remission time, no matter what he does, then, if a guard asks him to do the simplest of tasks, there is going to be no co-operation. Over time, this kind of legislation can tend to turn the internal
operations, particularly of maximum security institutions, into an absolutely impossible situation.
I took the opportunity a few years ago when I was in Mexico to go into some of what we would describe here in Canada as "user pay" maximum security institutions. It appears pretty Draconian when one walks in. There are machine guns everywhere. One feels if they make the wrong move they are going to "get it". I am sure that is how they operate in the periphery of those institutions. However, it is intriguing when one gets inside. Other than for maximum security, dangerous individuals who are kept in what we would call here "solitary confinement", the majority of the inmates are in fact at work producitively providing the capital and operational costs for those institutions. I think we should look more carefully at that kind of operation where the inmates make hammocks, shoes, are growing all their food and making the clothing for the guards and themselves. They are making all kinds of goods which are sold in the market-place in Mexico. The majority of the actual costs in some of the states in Mexico for the operation of their institutions is covered by work done by the inmates. The costs which are actually paid out are the costs for some parts of the construction of the physical plant and the costs of the guards so that they avoid at least some possibilities of corruption. Here in Canada, Mr. Speaker, to use this kind of "hot boxing" legislation is going to drive some of the best people out of the national parole service. They are already leaving. It is going to drive some of the best guards out of the system and we will be left with what is known in the vernacular with inmates as the "knuckle draggers". We will be left with a very unpredictable situation-something I do not believe Canadians want to see-and that is the armed forces having to move in to circle the circumference of all kinds of medium, minimum and maximum security institutions.
I feel this is a piece of legislation which can be modified to achieve the real concerns of the Canadian public. To move forward with such a narrowly worded Bill, particularly on parole and mandatory supservision provisions on gating and the revolving door syndrome, is very wrong. I hope that Parliament will respectfully study this Bill much more carefully.

subtopic: PAROLE ACT, PENITENTIARY ACT, PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES ACT, AND CRIMINAL CODE MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Certainly at the outset, 1 want you to know that I do not share the pessimism of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and I find it very difficult to understand the statement made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), when he said that crime would be increased by exercising greater control of the dangerous criminal.
It seems to me that it would be the exact opposite. That is one of the reasons I appreciate the support of my colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata), on this Bill. We think it is a good Bill. It is one which the Canadian public are requesting.
September 13, 1985

My colleague, the Eton. Member for Burnaby, does not seem to understand that at the present time many of the penitentiaries are now getting into agricultural projects; for instance, Bowden and the one in Prince Albert. They are starting to produce their own vegetables, dairy products and their own beef so that they will become self-sufficient and will not be an increasing burden on society generally. Perhaps we can cut down that $40,000 per year per person cost. I agree with my colleague, the Elon. Member for York South-Weston, when he said that many of our people do not necessarily need to be in prison because of the fact that they are not dangerous.
I believe that in that case, those who are convicted can pay their penalty to society by community projects. Therefore, they would not necessarily be a burden on society generally. That is why I am pleased to speak in favour of the passage of Bill C-67 and Bill C-68. Both are directed to bringing about necessary improvements to our system of criminal justice.
One of the major issues in our society today is to adequately protect from criminal activities the innocent person. There are far too many people who are frightened about their well-being because criminal activity is increasing in our society. There may be various reasons for this but, nevertheless, we have to accept it as fact. I am sure we can all agree that crime is a terrible thing. One way or another every Canadian is affected during his lifetime by criminal acts. Many become victims of crime and we all must bear the growing cost of police, courts and correctional programs. While it seems that crime may never be completely eliminated in a free society, it should never be tolerated. Canadians must be offered the best possible protection from crime at a cost we can afford. Therefore, the Government is committed to making our system of criminal justice as effective as possible rather than simply expanding its parameters and costs. The Bills now before the House are part of this process.
Those who have advocated the abolition of mandatory supervision with apparent disregard for the cost of such a move make a very erroneous assumption. They contend that the program is based on leniency but nothing could be further from the truth. In Canada, as in virtually all western nations, inmates have been allowed to earn remission of their sentence for over a century. Good time, as it is often called, has been a part of our system since 1868. For most of that time inmates were simply released when the remission date was reached as though it was the actual end of the sentence. In 1970, mandatory supervision was introduced. From then on every penitentiary inmate who was not paroled earlier was subject to the control and direction of a parole supervisor after being released due to remission. These additional conditions applied to approximately 70 per cent of released inmates who formerly went out free and clear.
It is important to emphasize that half of those who have their mandatory supervision revoked and are returned to penitentiary may not have committed a new crime. They are returned because their parole supervisors believe their behaviour indicates a risk of re-offending and this preventive step is
Criminal Code Amendments
in order. Before mandatory supervision existed they would have gone on to commit the crime before being apprehended. On the other hand, many of those who do not commit a new offence do not do so because their positive re-adjustment to community life has been assisted by their supervisor. Ultimately, the vast majority of inmates will return to the community, whether it is on full parole, mandatory supervision or simply because their sentence has expired. The best long term protection that can be offered in these cases is their successful return to a law-abiding lifestyle. For most this is far more likely with a gradual re-entry during which assistance and control is provided. The extra surveillance provided by this period also makes it more likely that developing problems will be foreseen and preventive action taken.
With experience, however, two major defects have become apparent with this program. Even where the need for preventive action is clear before release, we are compelled to release inmates on mandatory supervision when the release date arrives. Secondly, even where inmates demonstrate their inability to profit from mandatory supervision and it is revoked, they continue to earn remission in penitentiary and we are compelled to release them again, sometimes repeatedly, until they reach the end of their sentence. I am very happy to say that Bill C-67 will correct these defects where inmates who have committed crimes of violence are concerned. 1 hasten to point out, Mr. Speaker, that some will say that this Bill will abolish earned remission. That is not the case. Inmates will continue to earn remission as before as long as they behave. However, earned remission has never meant the shortening of the sentence imposed by the court. What this Bill does is remove the automatic right to release as a result of having earned remission. It creates in its stead a presumptive release subject to review by the National Parole Board. The Board is empowered by this Bill to withhold this release only if it can determine after a fair and exhaustive process that the inmate is likely to commit a violent act while under supervision. This becomes a case of reverse onus.
Because the inmate has earned remission and therefore been given a presumed release date, he will be released until it can be determined that he or she will be a danger to society. I would argue that this retains the impact of earned remission which some feel is important to maintain institutional order, but removes the most illogical part of the present arrangement, the automatic nature of the release without the exercise of any judgment. The corrective measures being proposed will by no means end violence perpetrated by former inmates. Unfortunately, the behavioural sciences are not yet at a point where human behaviour can accurately be predicted, but they do allow us to intervene in those cases where there is good cause to perceive a threat to the public. This will provide an additional measure of protection in a responsible and cost effective fashion.
I would now like to turn briefly to the difficult question of predicting violence. The Hon. Member for Burnaby has pointed out that no study anywhere has shown it is possible to predict violence. He has also stated that studies carried out in

September 13, 1985
Criminal Code Amendments
the Department of the Solicitor General have recommended against the use of methods of prediction in relation to violent crime and he is absolutely right. It is exactly for these reasons that we have moved away from the prediction of violence to the assessment of risk. A small number of inmates have so many characteristics pointing to violent behaviour that in our opinion it is more acceptable that a few inmates suffer some loss of freedom rather than letting the public carry the risk of an extremely violent or fatal crime. We agree that science cannot help us out of this problem but the lack of scientific certainty does not eliminate the fact that Parliament has a responsibility to decide who is going to be protected, the inmates or the public. This is a very important point in this Bill. This proposed legislation does not protect the public at any price, nor does it protect the inmate at any price; it represents a balanced protection of both sides.
In order to fully understand the critical point of balance, I have to explain that what you have in front of you will not stand alone. We are now developing carefully formulated regulations which clearly outline what kind of inmates will be detained until the expiry of their sentence. The regulations will also contain all the procedures to safeguard the inmates' rights in this respect. The criteria will be so stringent that there will be little danger of abuse by the National Parole Board. We are far from lending the Parole Board any sweeping powers. If anything, the Parole Board's discretion in this area will be more limited than in any other. The people we want to keep in prison are those serving a sentence for a crime of violence which has caused death or serious harm to the victim. In addition, we will require a persistent pattern of violence in the offender's past or clinical assessments which conclude there is an imminent risk of highly violent behaviour if the offender is released. Finally, the new regulations will allow us to prevent automatic release when we know that the inmate is planning a murder or a crime causing serious harm. It is these three groups of violent people that we are talking about and none other. I am convinced that the small number of offenders that we have in mind are not going to add to our overcrowding problem, nor will this legislation create institutional unrest. The inmates will know how few will be affected.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, if we can keep some of those people who are not dangerous to society out of prisons and let them pay their penalty through community projects, we will move in a direction which will be to the benefit of society generally. Even if the application will be narrow, the increase in public protection will be substantial. We count on our colleagues in all Parties to give their best advice during committee work in order to obtain the best possible protection for all Canadians and the highest degree of fairness to inmates.
This Bill is far above political manoeuvering. It is too important to play politics with because we are talking about the protection of the public and the well-being of those who have been convicted. I am pleased to say that we have already received expressions of support for these measures from a
number of community groups and individuals, including an organization of victims of crime. This support is very welcome since we are increasingly aware of the needs of victims and the importance of the views of groups such as this. Victims have long been the silent and forgotten participant in the criminal justice system, but those days are at an end. The Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) has recently helped fund several conferences of victims' groups and such efforts will continue so that the interests of victims will be more clearly expressed and listened to.
We are equally concerned about potential victims, Mr. Speaker. With the leadership and assistance of the Ministry of the Solicitor General, a number of crime prevention and crime awareness initiatives have been undertaken around the country with demonstrably positive results. These initiatives will continue.
We are also concerned that those charged with the onerous duty of dealing with convicted offenders on a day-to-day basis be given the tools they need to do the job. Bill C-68 is a modest beginning to modernize the correctional law an eliminate technical obstacles to understandable and efficient correctional programs. The amendments contained in this Bill will help modernize and streamline legislation bearing on both federal and provincial correctional systems and will be welcomed by correctional workers in both jurisdictions.
In view of the positive and needed features of both of these Bills, I recommend their speedy passage to members of the House. In the few minutes remaining for debate today, I hope that Members will see fit to give this Bill second reading in order that it can go to committee have we will have the opportunity to question witnesses who are interested in better control of criminals.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the previous speaker to comment on a point which he, the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), and the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) touched on. Under the present system some people are released who may commit violent crimes and, in fact, some of them have done so. Under the proposed system those people would be kept in for the full term of their sentence. If we begin this system in the fall of 1985 an inmate with two or three years yet to serve will be held back for that period of time. As the previous speaker said, society will be protected from him for that time, but eventually he will get out. In fact, he will be released at the same time as a number of other people. There will be an extra surge of people being released at the same time and they will be no less violent than they may be now. If they would be inclined to commit violent crimes if released on mandatory supervision now, they will be so inclined then.
Will the Hon. Member explain why he thinks they will be less violent when released at that time? Even if he does not agree that there would be a surge because of the change in timing, he cannot deny that there would be the same potential for violence after release. If anything, that potential will be increased by the frustration of denial, perhaps even in a person who was not previously considered potentially violent. Why does the Hon. Member believe that society will be protected
September 13, 1985

against violent people who will go directly out on to the streets?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the correctional system is working toward the rehabilitation of people who are going back into society. The House resumed from Monday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cassidy:
That the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates be empowered to study the question of granting to federal public employees the full political participation enjoyed by other Canadians and, that the Committee report its findings to the House no later than June 28, 1985.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I started this speech on Monday, April 15, 1985 and at that time had an opportunity to do nothing more than introduce the subject. I appreciate the opportunity to resume the discussion. I appreciate that the motion may appear to be stale-dated, but I understand that it is going to be up-dated after I am finished. I suggest the debate can continue on the theory of whether or not this goes to a committee, without worrying at this time about the date "June 30, 1985".
My remarks mainly concern the implications of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the time honoured tradition of impartiality in the Public Service. As the House knows, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees freedom of expression, freedom of association, the right to vote and the right to be qualified for membership not only in the House of Commons but in a legislative assembly of one of
Public Service
the provinces or territories. This right is guaranteed to everyone, including employees of the Public Service of Canada.
I believe we are all aware that if there are to be any limitations to these rights and freedoms, it must be demonstrated that they are reasonable limits that are justifiable in a free and democratic society in which we live.
Historically, our Public Service at all levels has operated on a non-political and impartial basis within the Canadian political and administrative context. Merit was the wole determinate of whether or not one is employed or advances. This concept has certainly evolved in recent decades and we are now at the point where there is a tradition of non-political bias and non-partisanship within the Public Service.
In the interests of an impartial, efficient and professional Public Service, there have been restraints placed on the capacity of public servants to take an active part in the public partisan politics and to express themselves publicly on matters of government concern. The Chair will know that the Supreme Court of Canada has presently reserved its decision on the appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal in Fraser versus Public Service Staff Relations Board. This appeal, brought by a former public servant, addresses exactly what participation is allowed and whether it impairs his or her ability to carry out their duties.
Partisan political activity of public servants is dealt with in Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. It states that no employee shall engage in, work for, on behalf of or against a political party or a candidate for election. It permits public servants to attend political meetings, make contributions to a candidate or political party. Public servants can also seek nomination as a candidate for election if they receive a clearance or leave of absence from the Public Service Commission. When the charter was proclaimed, it brought into question the nature and the application of any restraints on the rights of public servants to freedom of speech and freedom of association with respect to political activities. We were all aware that when the Charter was implemented it would give rise to a challenge to the traditional view, as it should, of the rights of public servants. That is the challenge we are concerned with now. Not only is the House of Commons dealing with this issue, the provinces and the territories are considering it from different perspectives. The first is to balance the ability of a person to have that freedom of association with the need to ensure that we maintain a Public Service that can serve in a neutral and impartial manner. Therefore, we must examine the restrictions that exist and make sure that we can justify them in our society.
Our democratic system is designed to serve people in their best interests. Therefore, no matter what political party is in power, we need a Public Service which can administer the programs of the Government of the day in a professional and neutral manner. We need a Public Service that can provide impartial advice and information to whatever political party is in power.
The question that this raises is one of perception. If we allow the Public Service to participate in the political activity-

In any event, in keeping with the traditions and demands that we have political neutrality, we set up some protections for public servants with which I believe we all agree.
I am not talking about tangible protections but such things as protection from unwarranted dismissal. Great improvements have been made in the Public Service Commission to ensure that there is no harrassment in any way because of one's opinions. There is also protection from what is called capricious career decisions and a guarantee that advancement
is based on merit, which is a guarantee that is fundamental to this debate. These guarantees give public servants protection that they can serve without any concerns that their job might be based on political partisanship. We are very serious about maintaining those guarantees, just as we are serious about maintaining the perception of neutrality.
I want to close by saying that the public perception is justs as important as the realization that public servants act in an impartial and neutral manner. I can tell the House that the matter which is the subject of this motion is the subject of active debate by the Government and is being considered. We treat our election promises very seriously and we do not in any way back down from them. We would not wish to back down from any promise or suggestion made during an election campaign. As the Member who defected from the provincial Liberal Party well knows, as Mr. Peterson well knows, we are not abolishing Ontario hospital premiums and we are not able to buy beer and liquor in corner grocery stores because things do not happen overnight. This matter is under active consideration. For that reason when my friend with whom 1 have had some consultation rises to amend the motion, he will find that myself, as a private Member, will be in support of the motion to change the date from June 30, 1985, to June 30, 1986, so that more people can be heard.
I know the Liberal Party has suppressed rights for public servants for the last 16 years and it has not given them any opportunity to enter these debates, having ruled out consideration of this matter on a serious basis, but 1 do hope the Liberals will go along with this amendment about to be proposed so we can have a proper debate. The one Member from the Liberal Party who is here may or may not be disposed to give his assent. 1 hope as a sort of break from the past and from character he could elevate his thinking and, in a sort of magnanimous gesture of perhaps seeing the light, see his way clear after consultation with the rest of his colleagues to support the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate on the resolution by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). At the outset, I want to compliment him for the resolution and for the many years he has fought for the political rights of public servants, both at the provincial level in Ontario and at the national level in this House. It is to his credit and also to the credit of many other Hon. Members in this place and in provincial legislatures across the country who have fought for that principle.
I want to say to my friend, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), yes, I will move a minor amendment to the resolution at the closing of my remarks. There have been discussions and I understand all three Parties are disposed to accepting the amendment because it is purely a matter of detail in terms of the House dealing with the resolution.
It has got to the point where, at the federal level and in the case of a few of the provinces that the people of Canada, the
September 13, 1985

Constitution and the Charter of Rights are now way ahead of this House of Commons. Political right is always supposed to have been a right. That is exactly what it means and that means a right is indivisible.
I will endeavour to be very non-partisan in this kind of a debate because it has been obvious for the last several years that all three political Parties, and Members in this Chamber from all Parties, support the security of the political rights of members of the public service and employees of federal Crown corporations.
I must say that under the first Premier of a democratic socialist Government on this continent in 1945, among the first half a dozen things it did as a new Government in my province was to enshrine in the statutes of that province not only a provincial Bill of Rights, but the rights of the public civil servants and the Crown corporations to organize, to join a union, to have collective bargaining rights and to have full political rights. That was in 1945 and I am proud of that. I am sure my colleagues in the other Parties will understand and forgive or appreciate my pride in that. Subsequent to that, I think at least four other provinces of other political Parties adopted similar or the same kinds of provisions in their jurisdictions. There is no longer any point in arguing as between political Parties or on a partisan basis about the necessity to make certain that federal public servants and Crown corporation employees have and may exercise at their discretion their political rights. It is an academic discussion now with the Charter of Rights in place.
I need only to quote the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was Leader of the Opposition-I accept his word and I believe the Hon. Member for Simcoe North and that is why I say it is no longer a partisan issue-who said:
We believe that this matter should be addressed by an all-party parliamentary committee in consultation with public service organizations-
That is exactly the purport of the resolution by my colleague, the Member for Ottawa Centre. To continue with the quote:
We believe the situation can be quickly resolved.
The then Leader of the Opposition went on to say that restrictions on public service political activity:
-are unnecessary and may not be justifiable under the terms of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
It is no longer a case of may not. They are not any longer justifiable under the terms of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This Parliament, and whoever happens to be governing, is now faced with the certainty that if an individual public civil servant or Crown corporation employee or their organization takes the Government or the Public Service Commission to court-and all they have to do is wave the directive sent out almost annually about political activity to all public service employees-the Government of the day and the Parliament of Canada will lose.

There will be some who may say after I sit down that "well, this matter is now before the courts; and this matter is now part of the collective bargaining process between the Government of Canada and the Public Service Commission". On this issue there is no bargaining. The fundamental rights of citizens and the matter of who employs them-and that includes political rights-are not negotiable. I submit that there are no limitations to political rights. I appreciate that 99 per cent of the time senior public servants who are appointed by Order in Council will not exercise their political rights because of their positions. However, that decision should be the decision of the senior public servant involved.
The Hon. Member for Simcoe North talked about political neutrality. He referred to the promise of his Party prior to entering the election dealing with the political rights of public servants. I believe him. I accept it. I agree that my hon. friends and colleagues in the Conservative Party are sincere in that promise. However, I wonder whether the Hon. Member, who is Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board, has any updated information on the initiatives taken by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to implement the promise made by his political Party regarding political rights.
Mention was made of the British Public Service. We all have to admit that it is much more professional than ours. Their public servants at the middle and senior levels make it a practice to be fully informed on the political policies of each Party. Whenever one of them takes power, senior public servants, deputy ministers and what not are able to approach the new Ministers to tell them about the policies and to give them several options on how to go about dealing with them. In that manner they act in a neutral fashion, but that does not gainsay that they have not exercised their political rights in their hours off duty.
The same applies here in Canada. A public servant, or for that matter an employee of a private corporation, may exercise his political rights in his own home, on his own property or in his own hours off duty. In fact, I had this experience as an employee of Canadian Pacific. I am sure Hon. Members understand that there is no particular love lost between CPR and the New Democratic Party. However, in my years of employment with that corporation, I carried out my duties in my hours on duty and after, when off duty, I went out and opposed its policies. I spoke on public platforms and was a candidate. I always received a leave of absence and always returned to my job. Perhaps the voters were too smart; I lost the first two times I ran! I always returned to my job. There was no harassment. The same applies to public servants.
We had better move fast on this because if we do not the courts will be ahead of us. We all know that. It is now academic in terms of the arguments which take place in this Chamber. The resolution of my colleague and my Private Member's Bill, which was debated in 1981 and again in 1984, apply to the same matter. I urge the House to adopt this

resolution so that the committee can begin to study it. I am quite prepared to withdraw my Bill from the Order Paper, and the Government House Leader can include an Order referring the subject matter of my Bill to the same committee which will deal with the resolution of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre. This means that the waterfront would be covered this fall and early winter. Then we could return to the Chamber for an all-Party or unanimous approval of the matter of political rights for a certain segment of our society. We are on very shaky and loose ground when we deny a fundamental right to one group while other groups have it.
In conclusion, I should like to move the following amendment, seconded by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse):
That the motion be amended by deleting the year "1985" and inserting the year "1986".
I do that to bring the Order Paper up to date. It is merely a detail; it changes one number from a five to a six. If the House approves the resolution and it is referred to the appropriate committee, members of that committee will have until the end of June next year to examine this matter in consultation with concerned public servants, their organizations, Members of the Government and members of the Public Service Commission, and then report back to the House with draft legislation or recommendations or whatever. I think they can accomplish that well in advance of the end of June, 1986. In any event, I understand from the discussions I have had that the amendment is acceptable and will not require any debate.
In closing, I urge my colleagues on all sides of the House to keep in mind that all of us have some responsibility to catch up to what is now the law of the land. Everyone knows that federal public servants and Crown corporation employees must have political rights. I hope this matter will receive quick passage and be referred to the appropriate committee.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to participate in this debate this
afternoon not only as a former public servant but, more important, as a servant or employee of the House.
This issue is a very important one for people who are called upon or choose to pursue occupations wherein they work for the Government of Canada, an agency of the Government or a Crown corporation. Of course this issue has been raised many times over the past number of years. I should like to draw the attention of the House to Chapter 11 of the so-called d'Avig-non Report which is better known as the Report of the Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and Merit Principles. That particular chapter refers to political participation. I must say that during the election campaign many public servants lobbied me to find out whether 1 agreed with the recommendations contained in that particular report. I must say that having been in the situation myself as an employee of this House in an administrative capacity, a capacity in which I was not called upon to work on a direct basis with members of various political Parties, I wished many times that I could have participated more fully in the political process. Obviously, as 1 am sure you have guessed by now, Mr. Speaker, I still did participate. Otherwise I would never have become not only a municipal councillor but a provincial Member as well as a federal Member if I had not commenced some kind of political activity while I was a member of the staff of the House of Commons.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the regulations that apply to public servants generally do not necessarily apply in all cases to the staff of the House of Commons. At least they did not when I worked here. There was some leeway given to me or rather some things were tolerated regarding the political activities in which I engaged as carefully as I could at the time.
In speaking to many friends who work in the Public Service, I find there are many things which public servants wonder about in relation to their rights. They wonder just what they are permitted to do at the present time as a federal public servant. Is it permitted for a public servant to erect a political sign on their lawn at the present time?

speechtext: It should be.

Of course it should be, as the Hon. Member has said, and no one is disagreeing with that. However, at present there is a tremendous amount of fear felt by some public servants. In the case of a couple, one of whom works for the Public Service and one of whom does not, I suppose the case could always be made that the sign belongs to the individual spouse who does not work for the Public Service. People who live alone or people who live together but both happen to be public servants have more difficulty at the present time.
What about public servants knocking on doors? Are they or are they not permitted to knock on doors for a political
September 13, 1985

candidate at this time? That question has been raised by various people. There have been various interpretations of the issue. People are really unsure about where they stand. When people are unsure, particularly in an era of high unemployment, they do not take a chance. People do not take a chance because they do not want to be fired and lose their jobs. That is the sad case of public servants at the present time.
Undoubtedly, the laws must be clarified. Individuals have to be given their rights. In so doing, it must be explained in a very clear way just what it is that they are permitted to do. For instance, the British system is composed of what is known as tiers. There is a certain category of individuals on which there are no restrictions, another category on which there are restrictions that can be removed by request and, as I understand it, another category of public servants who are prohibited from participating in the political process in a similar way that all public servants in Canada are prohibited. The three-category system in Britain may not be perfect, but it is certainly a long way away from what we have now.
Perhaps I could mention a specific example. What political implication could there possibly be and what prohibition should there be for someone who works as a truck driver for the Department of Supply and Services knocking on doors for a political candidate in the evenings? Obviously there is no political implication in that case. That should be properly recognized.
I would like to refer to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis). The Hon. Member indicated that it was his Party that had promised during the election campaign to find a solution to this particular problem and to lift restrictions from public servants in this country. A letter from the now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the then Leader of the Opposition, was sent to Mr. Jack Donegani of the PIPs group of public servants in which he said that the PC Party believes that the present restrictions on political activities are unnecessary and likely not justifiable under the terms of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. While the rights of some senior public servants must be restricted in order to prevent conflict of interest, we feel that this issue could be addressed without disenfranchising over 200,000 public servants in the process.
It has been over a year since the Government was elected. That was one of the promises that was made along with a number of others. I have here my little booklet which I have shown to you upon occasion, Mr. Speaker. This booklet is entitled 338 Tory Promises. The Hon. Member for Simcoe North said that the promises could not all be kept in the first year. I agree with him, but I have calculated that at the present rate, it will take until the year 2026 before all the promises are delivered.

speechtext:
I think the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is quite familiar with the procedure in speaking to amendments. In fact, I have seen the New Democratic Party use that procedure as a means of filibuster for days and days and weeks and weeks on end.
The essence of allowing a review by the Government and a report back by the Government between September 1985 and June 1986 with respect to whether or not public servants should have full political rights is an important issue. I have no difficulty with the general thrust. I spoke on the issue when it was put forward by the Hon. Member for Regina West, I believe, back in the fall. On that occasion I believe the Hon. Member was extremely pleased. In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) came into the Chamber during Private Members' Hour. As the Hon. Member for Regina West pointed out, in his 17 years of being in this place it was the first time he had seen a Prime Minister come in and sit through a debate during Private Members' Hour. It can be noted that he picked the debate on full political rights to public servants as the debate to which he wished to listen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
I know you did. I know that the Prime Minister is serious in the commitment he made during the campaign. Although the previous speaker indicated he believed political promises or commitments would not be implemented, I believe I can honestly say that we have implemented more political commitments than the federal Liberal Party ever did. What I can say is that we have not had the temerity to stand up, as did
one of the senior people in the provincial Liberal Party and say, as Robert Nixon did-he just left and abandoned it- "We will not be able to fill our political promises now." That is what he said at the first opportunity he had when he was addressing some of the issues after he became Treasurer. We have not said that. We believe we will be able to fill our political promises during the four or five years of our mandate. I think this is one which will be carried out.
It is important to note that there have been some detailed discussions on a number of matters going on with the public service unions. Those matters have not been concluded. We hope they will be concluded prior to June 30, 1986, However, they were somewhat delayed after some initial announcements last April dealing with master contracts and about four different topics dealing with pensions and so on. At that time, they said one of the items which was on the table but not yet being discussed was the issue which is a substantive part of the motion before us; that is to say, public servants have full rights.
This is, by and large, a non-partisan issue, as long as it is dealt with prior to the next election.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext: That long?

speechtext:
It will not have much of a meaningful effect as long as it is done before the next election.
I would like to see them given the full opportunity of defining the ramifications of this point within the negotiations. For example, in the United Kingdom, which 1 had the opportunity to visit earlier this year, I asked how they defined the situation. They have broken the Public Service in the United Kingdom into three tiers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext: Only three tiers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Unfortunately, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) is always barking. We hear him so frequently. He is like a mad terrier. 1 guess he does not like to hear other people's thoughts. He likes to hear only his own voice. So be it.
As I was trying to say, in England they have broken the Public Service into three tiers. The First tier has absolute full political rights. The second tier, which is more or less the middle-management tier, has limited political rights but more political rights than what we have in Canada under the present legislation. The top tier, which includes deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers and associate deputy ministers, does not have political rights.
I think it only appropriate for the discussions to continue with the various public service unions in order to define the ramifications. Hopefully, in the next few months they will get over their discussions on master contracts. Hopefully, they will have dealt with the discussions on indexation of pensions and how they should be indexed. I hope they will move on to these two topics which are on the table but which have not yet received full discussion. I feel confident that they, in their
September 13, 1985

wisdom, might come up with a solution which will be acceptable to all parties.
The Hon. Member for Regina West has indicated that the courts will decide this matter for us. It may well be that there will be a decision in the Fraser case which will decide the issue by and large. However, there are some things, such as Section 1 of the Charter of Rights, which allow for certain limitations. I think the court will have to make a decision on whether or not this is a reasonable limitation. Indeed, if the court was so well convinced right off the cuff that it was just, it would not have reserved its decision. It would have announced its decision from the bench on the occasion of the adjournement of the hearing. However, it has reserved because there are a few more matters to deal with other than the granting carte blanche to everybody of free political rights, whether they be a Deputy Minister or a unionized person who is a clerk.
Having said that, it would be helpful to see whether the Government, as the employer, and the unions on behalf of the employees, can perhaps appropriately define this issue. I suggest we have limited time in which we can deal with the issue. If they fail to address the matter within the next year, then I imagine this will become a bit of a hot potato. I imagine the matter will be spoken to by various people with some meaning, dedication and conviction.

It would be a lot better if he were more appreciative and sat back and listened to other people for a change. If he wants to seek the floor he can seek the floor and stand up and speak for his allotted time. Until then, maybe he should learn to shut up.
Public Service
I think this is a very sensitive issue; it is a partisan issue. When we were in opposition we called for full political rights. During the election campaign we called for full political rights.
I feel very strongly about it because I was a public servant who was fired from his job because I sought a political nomination back in 1972. I felt that I was improperly disenfranchised. I should say that I was not disenfranchised because I insisted on exercising my franchise, but I felt afterwards that I was improperly fired from my job as a public servant because I took the action I thought was appropriate.
No doubt there are people on all sides of the House who feel very strongly about this issue. I just caution all Hon. Members, that rather than using rhetoric to inflame the issue, give the Government proper time. There was a delay in the negotiations from April on because one of the largest public sector unions had an election in June and there was some difference of opinion leading up to that election as to what they had agreed to in April. I believe that has been resolved and the union is now back bargaining with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) on behalf of the Government as the employer. I believe they will be moving on this. If they do not resolve it, then I believe it will become a hot political issue, and it should become so. I am hoping they will resolve this. I do not believe the courts are going to rule ahead of us, but if they do, so be it. The next federal election is about three and a half to four years away. The next provincial election is-

And we intend to implement our promises during the period of time we have.
As to the next provincial election, we have been promised by the bed mates, the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party in the Province of Ontario, that there is not going to be one for two years. There may be other areas which are interested in this. I live in Ontario. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell who is squawking over there could have addressed this issue during his speech a few minutes ago. He decided not to. I think we have to keep calm about it because it is an emotional topic for many people. It can be inflamed so easily by rhetoric, with everything being put off track. I just hope that does not happen.
If it is apparent towards the end of the Government's term in office that we have failed to come through with it, then I believe we are open for every attack in the world. In the meantime, I hope we will try to let the employers and employees work out in an amicable fashion the demarcation lines, where exactly this should begin, and the extent and how far up the scale within the Public Service they should go for full political rights. I believe they should go very far up the scale. I do have problems, perhaps, with Deputy Ministers, Assistant Deputy Ministers, and so on, but I feel this is open for negotiation.
I want to thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to make this contribution. I must admit that I do not agree with the date the Government set to report back, June of 1986.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). I agree it is time to stop debating this issue. Everyone agrees that our public servants should have the same political rights as their fellow citizens.
We have also discussed at length the whole complexity of the kind of solution we should seek. I agree with my hon. friend from Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) that we should not set a deadline, since negotiations are being held. On the other hand, I do not think we should leave it up in the air. I feel we should really consider some way of, for instance, having the issue brought before a committee of the House, while making it quite clear when the proposal is made to do so, that the process should not prejudice the negotiations taking place between the unions and Treasury Board. This is not a frivolous matter, it is indeed a very serious one, because I am particularly interested in the depoliticizing of public servants and of the public service.
I have been in Parliament for only a year, Mr. Speaker, and I have already had some experience, unfortunately, of the far too politicized state of our public service. In projects that were
really necessary and that were supposed to contribute to the development of certain industrial sectors and regions, some public service employees, who were used to working with certain people in the community, seem to want to retain a certain decision-making power that is not really theirs. So it is extremely urgent to depoliticize the public service.
As far as the merit principle is concerned, every week I get calls or letters from public service employees in my riding who write: Mrs. Mailly, I was a CR-2, or I was a CR-3, I could have had a promotion, I had a very good performance appraisal report, but someone else was appointed who was slipped into the system. There is favoritism within the public service, a situation that probably started at one time as a result of political pressure and which today has become firmly rooted in the public service.
I think this is very bad for the rights of employees and for a public service that claims to serve the public. Mr. Speaker, I say let us stop looking at all the angles of this subject, let negotiations between the unions and the Treasury Board proceed, but please, let us not wait another year to solve this problem! I think that the date suggested by my hon. friend from Regina West is not soon enough.
